This trend is linked to changes in nuclear radii caused by intruder configurations. Recent findings from gamma-ray spectroscopy on 64Ni enable an in-depth analysis of its structure. This paper focuses on the ground state band of 64Ni and investigates the potential for form coexistence within its even-even isotopic series. An investigation into the tensor operator's influence in the ground state band of 64Ni yields an interesting result: although the tensor operator has a significant impact, it has zero net effect due to the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov state being at zero spin. Consequently, we propose that form coexistence in 64Ni is driven by the monopole tensor interaction.

Chiral theories in four-dimensional SUSY quantum field theory are an intriguing area, as they may exhibit duality, a characteristic of non-superscript theories. We have made a preliminary attempt to identify potential dual pairs among a set of chiral Sp(2N) gauge theories with various superfields. Although a comprehensive duality verification is still required, our analysis shows dualities in specific cases, particularly those involving fundamental and adjoint matter, particularly when N takes on even or odd values.

This study establishes a direct method to construct linear complementary sets of group codes over finite principal ideal fields, and proves an condition for when these linear complementary sets exist. Furthermore, it gives specific examples of codes that have codes over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ as their images, demonstrating that the linear complementary sets of group codes are not always equivalent to those in the paper by Kurihara, Matsumoto, and Tonomura.

Constrained optimization of a joint function can be tackled by converting it into a maximization problem for a restricted function whose size depends on the constraints specified. When this restricted function is identified correctly, the problem becomes a standard maximum likelihood estimation (MPE) task. Identifying the restricted function is equivalent to determining the maximum-entropy distribution within a specified class. We demonstrate that, in graphical models with specific constraints, such as those defining certain patterns, this distribution can be calculated exactly and its structure represented efficiently using a particular type of expression. Our approach also provides a way to calculate a lower bound on the size of the restricted function and, more broadly, we show that any function's behavior under constraints can be determined using an iterative procedure based on a widely used optimization technique.

Many service sector employees face challenges when clients leave items behind upon departure.
Although detecting and identifying these items is crucial for the staff, current methods are largely ineffective.
To address this issue, we introduce DropFind, an AI-based system that employs machine learning and computer vision to automatically alert staff members when an item is discarded.
DropFund leverages the power of audio-visual sensors to capture both visual and auditory data, which are then used to train a deep learning model that identifies instances of item discarding.
Our system has been evaluated in a real-world setting and the staff members equipped with DropFind's item-dropping detection functionality demonstrated improved efficiency.

In recent years, there has been a surge of research focusing on the collective properties of dense particle assemblies. A notable subset of this research involves materials exhibiting shear thickening, where viscosity increases with applied stress. The core objective of this paper is to identify universal characteristics of the shear thickening transition, which emerges from collective behaviors. Our findings, derived from experiments and computer simulations, demonstrate that the spatial and temporal scales associated with the transition can be normalized using material-specific parameters. Furthermore, the study reveals a combined master curve when normalizing both stress and material parameters, which is a first in this field. The implications of this discovery are that the critical exponents of the shear thickening transition can be more accurately determined.

This research aims to fill a gap in current literature by analyzing the distribution and hourly consumption patterns of electricity in Bangladesh. Given the lack of available data, this study simulates a probability distribution that fits electricity consumption data, and develops hourly consumption models based on typical daily profiles.

This study investigates how individuals' Google account settings, which tailor search results based on personal preferences, affect their browsing behavior and the content they encounter online. We tested this by exposing participants to a Google search without providing any explicit information, and found that the search engine's personalization can inadvertently override any explicit knowledge they possess. Our research demonstrates that the way Google's search engine is customized can inadvertently skew individuals' perceptions, and that the effects compound as more personalized search results are provided. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the personalization settings can cause a decline in the quality of decisions made by participants, and that the effects are more pronounced among individuals who rely heavily on Google for information. This study contributes to a broader understanding of how the way Google's search engine is customized can influence individuals' perceptions and behaviors, and that the effects can influence their ability to learn and make informed decisions.

Program synthesis is the process of automatically generating correct programs
based on specific requirements, and one effective approach to this problem
involves using graphs to represent programs, allowing for easier manipulation
and synthesis. Current graph-based synthesis methods utilize graphs that include
nodes with node types to convey more information, but this can lead to issues
when some node types are more frequently present in solution graphs than others.
To address this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning method that focuses
on identifying crucial graph connections by using a graph-based convolutional neural
network to synthesize programs from flow diagrams.

Despite significant advancements in climate and atmospheric general circulation models (GCMs/GRMs), achieving optimal results remains challenging due to the vast computational requirements of Earth-system simulations. To overcome this obstacle, a variety of dimention-reduction methods have been developed and integrated into climate models, including those targeting cloud modeling, temporal modeling, and modeling the atmosphere itself. This paper reviews the techniques of dimention-reduction, highlighting their benefits and drawbacks, and explores potential applications in climate and Earth-system modeling to improve computational efficiency.

We've compiled detailed atomic data for specific O$^7+$-like ions, including Au$^{4+}$ and a sequence with osmium, by performing relativistic calculations. These findings provide essential information regarding the opacity of kilonova ejecta.

Radiation oncologists' goal is to have tumor-bearing areas receive maximum radiation while minimizing surrounding healthy tissue exposure. Advanced techniques like intensity-modulated radiation therapy and proton beam therapy allow this, but require precise tissue segmentation for accurate dose delivery. Radiologists' manual segmentation can be time-consuming and prone to errors, but deep learning-based methods can improve this process, especially when trained on data from related medical imaging tasks. This research presents an approach to trained deep neural networks for abdominal organ segmentation, adapted from maxillary sinus detection in CT scans, and evaluates its performance on a dataset of stomach and liver images.

This project's goal is to achieve clarity and understanding in information analysis through interactive exploration and visual representation, employing advanced linear algebra techniques such as matrix factorization and graph theory while maintaining a holistic perspective.

A comprehensive review of all confirmed exoplanets in the CORALIE/HARPS discovery sample has been performed. Initially, we calculated each planet's radius by dividing the stellar radius of its host star with the estimated radius of the planet. Subsequently, we analyzed the correlation between the radii of planets with radii less than 10 Earth radii and those with masses less than 10 Jupiter masses, taking into account the radiation they receive from their host stars. We discovered that the sample does not exhibit a distinct desert area, as previously suggested. We then investigated the potential reasons behind this by comparing the characteristics of the CORALIE/HARPS exoplanets to those of the ARIES/HIRES and APOGEE/MIKE exoplanets, which showed a clear presence of a desert area. We discovered that the CORALIE/HARPS exoplanets are predominantly short-period planets, and that their formation may be influenced by the migration and displacement of the planets from their original locations. We also found that the CORALIE/HARPS exoplanets are mostly composed of rock and ice, and that their formation may be similar to that of the ARIES/HIRES and APOGEE/MIKE exoplanets, which are characterized by a higher water content.

This study suggests an effective approach to enhance representation learning by explicitly considering attention regulation during the training process. The method strives to maximize the sharing of crucial information about class labels across varying input conditions, thereby promoting robust attention mechanisms. By leveraging explicit constraints, the proposed approach clearly defines the attention mechanism's objectives. Our technique has been successfully applied to several image classification benchmarks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR50, and CIFAR100. The results indicate that the method significantly improves performance on these datasets. Furthermore, the ability to control attention mechanisms through post-training is a valuable asset. Our experiments confirm that this capability enables the model to prioritize essential visual features, thereby enhancing its explainability.

If dark matter interacts with ordinary matter through a mediating particle like a light scalar, vector, or spin-1/2 fermion, it's possible for dark matter to be significantly denser than previously thought. We introduce a simple model in which dark matter and a mediator particle are produced by an out-of-equilibrium event early in the universe, such as the decay of a heavy field. This model allows for the existence of dark matter halos on scales as small as the Earth, provided the dark matter mass is between $10^{-12}$ eV and $30$ keV. The dark matter density at these small scales could be up to $10^{24}$ times the critical density, potentially solving several astrophysical and cosmological issues. We explore the potential signs of such a dense dark matter distribution in three areas: potential differences in dark matter annihilation rates within and outside of the Earth, the formation of dark matter "clumps" due to bound states with the mediator particle, and the possibility of forming primordial black holes.

Closely connected neural circuits can adapt their connections to process new information more efficiently, reflecting a key aspect of brain plasticity. This concept is embodied in an artificial intelligence model, a simple yet flexible neural network, that can learn various cognitive tasks rapidly and maintain its learned abilities throughout the process. Despite its structural complexity, this model can be trained effectively using standard techniques, making its potential applications in understanding cognitive disorders more attainable.

We develop a framework to study infinite-dimensional nilpotent algebras with finite generators through the construction of a special variety. By analyzing algebraic equations, we establish connections to central nilpotence degrees and establish relationships with central sequences. Additionally, we derive specific geometric properties and demonstrate the applicability of this framework through examples, including the algebra of upper-triangular matrices and a specific quiver algebra.

High-speed jets from supermassive black holes are known to produce powerful electromagnetic radiation, as well as radiation that can be seen across a wide range of frequencies. This type of radiation is often associated with the activity of the black hole's accretion disk. The accuracy of observations and theoretical models is crucial in understanding the characteristics of this radiation, which can be affected by various physical processes. One such process is the interaction between the radiation and the cosmic microwave background, which can be a significant factor at certain redshifts and frequencies. This interaction can lead to increased radiation output at lower frequencies, a phenomenon that has been observed in the case of the quasar PDS456. This phenomenon is thought to be the result of a process called Compton scattering, which occurs when the radiation interacts with the electrons in the accretion disk. This process can transfer energy from the electrons to the photons, causing an increase in the radiation's energy and, consequently, an increase in the radiation's temperature. This effect can be observed as a "bump" in the radiation spectrum at a specific frequency, which can be detected as an excess of radiation above the thermal radiation that is typically produced by the accretion disk. This type of radiation is often associated with the activity of the black hole and can be used to study the physical processes that are taking place in the accretion disk and the jet.

This review covers various generalized lagrangians for classical general relativity. It also considers hyperbolic and elliptic structural properties, along with existence results for corresponding gauge theories, within the framework of the absolute gauge theory concept. Furthermore, high-order general relativity connections with quantum gravity correspondences are linked.

We have developed a novel approach for registering picture volumes with themselves, building on the existing method used for registering individual images. This approach utilizes 2D descriptors, either from SIFT or DS symmetry, to identify corresponding features within the volumes. By considering correlations between descriptors of adjacent slices, we are able to determine corresponding triplets of slices, effectively defining a correspondence map, and subsequently applying a 3D rigid transformation. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in terms of accuracy and robustness compared to alternative solutions, such as the method proposed by Torres et al, and shows particularly significant improvements over this existing solution for volumes characterized by low or variable scale features.

We analyzed photometric and spectroscopic data of the binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which has a 40.5-minute period. Using a combination of synthetic magnitudes and color indices, we created light and color curves for various bandpasses. By applying a radiative transfer code to synthetic atmospheres, which varied in temperature and electron density, we determined the effective temperatures and electron densities at different eclipse points. Our analysis revealed that the secondary star is hotter than the primary star, with a temperature of 12,000 K compared to 10,000 K. We also observed that the binary system exhibits a 4,000 K difference in temperature during various phases, which we attribute to an infrared excess. This excess is likely caused by the interaction between the stars, which forms a common envelope around the binary system.

Global aggregation methods, commonly used in machine learning and high-throughput screening, have significant limitations. They overlook connections between samples and assume uniform distribution, which can lead to a lack of insight into underlying data patterns. A proposed solution leverages the power of optimal transport to create an aggregation method that considers sample relationships and offers both an transport cost and a distance metric for evaluating distances. This new method comes with performance guarantees through a dual formulation and is supported by empirical testing that demonstrates its superiority over existing aggregation techniques on real-world data.

The characteristics of galaxies hosting different types of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are examined. Studies have revealed notable disparities in properties of early-type galaxies based on AGN type, particularly in star formation rates and dust content. However, such distinctions are not observed among late-type galaxies. Our analysis of the Spitzer Space Telescope's Third Data Release shows that host galaxies of various AGN types exhibit similar inclinations. In contrast, previous studies using compact radio sources indicated that hosts of type II AGN tend to be more edge-on. To explore this discrepancy, we compare the host galaxies of both radio and non-radio types I and II AGN, discovering that type II AGN hosted by dust-rich systems display the aforementioned trend, whereas types I do not exhibit this behavior in either sample.

This study focuses on submanifolds of E^4, an arbitrary dimension, featuring a flat rotation surface structure around a curve and a sphere, with the whole submanifolds classified if having a pointwise 1-type Gauss map.

This study investigates whether supervising a pre-trained model with depth is more effective than using classification, which has been the conventional approach. We present an in-depth analysis, comparing the advantages and limitations of these methods, and propose several strategies to enhance the performance of the d-based approach. Experimental results from our ANNOTATIONLESS challenge further confirm that using depth for pre-training is a more effective strategy, particularly when annotations are scarce.

Most applications of NLP are heavily dependent on domain-specific knowledge.
Significant advancements have been made in the field of time-series forecasting, yet current methods are confined to a single domain.
To bridge this gap, we propose TCube, a novel approach for learning time-series narratives.
TCube is a domain-independent, end-to-end framework that uses a transformer-based language model to describe temporal relationships in various time-series datasets.
We evaluate TCube on a set of six diverse, real-world datasets and demonstrate its superior performance in comparing with existing domain-adapted techniques.
Furthermore, TCube enables a new type of time-series analysis, as evidenced by a case study showcasing its effectiveness in uncovering insights from data.
TCube's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/TCube/TCube.

The ATLAS detector has been evaluating the Higgs boson's properties and exploring rare processes in other areas of research. This paper focuses on the study of rare phenomena associated with beauty mesons, specifically light neutral mesons. Investigations into these areas may provide insights into phenomena that cannot be explained by the Standard Model. The paper discusses four distinct analyses aimed at examining these unusual occurrences.
On a Cayley tree of arbitrary degree, we analyze the Ising model and find new types of periodic and mildly periodic measures that represent local correlations within the system.

This research expands on the work of Arsen'ev and Arutyunov (2015) and Arsen'ev et al. (2018), who studied hyperbolic Cauchy problems of a specific form. The current study proves that the coefficients of the principal part, which decrease at a log-sublinear rate as time increases, do not hinder the global solvability of the problem in $C^{2, \omega}$-function spaces, provided the function's decay is not excessive. The proof relies on the application of the method of majorants, using functions that decay in a specific manner, in conjunction with results from Arsen'ev and Arutyunov (2015) and Arsen'ev et al. (2018). The findings generalize the results of Lasiecka and Tretter (2009) and Arsen'ev and Arutyunov (2015) for the case of logarithmic decay.
Determining Word Boundaries in Continuous Japanese Text: A Proposed Strategy based on Morphological Analysis and Moby-2 Dictionary Lookup

Developers frequently seek assistance on the Stack Overflow platform when encountering technical difficulties.  A substantial portion of assistance requests involve links to external sources, which we have analyzed in this study by examining developers' links shared on Stack Overflow.  By collecting a large sample of 1.5 million external links provided by developers, we investigated which platforms these links are typically hosted on and which websites these developers visit.  By partnering with Google and using their tools and data, we were able to assess the quality and reliability of these links and the platforms hosting them.  Additionally, we explored the underlying reasons for developers' preferences for certain platforms based on our sharing behavior and the platforms' characteristics.  To provide more value to researchers and practitioners, we also created a publicly accessible database containing the collected links and their corresponding attributes.

There's a pressing requirement to understand the effects of galaxy evolution on models of the universe's expansion, particularly when analyzing recent observations. A critical issue arises because there's a lack of consistent data on how different types of galaxies evolve over time, which is essential for accurate understanding. A potential solution to this problem could involve utilizing a reliable dataset consisting of quasar galaxy companions, given that they can be easily identified and are likely representative of normal galaxies. In this study, the reliability of this dataset is thoroughly evaluated, and its suitability is confirmed. A preliminary analysis reveals that its data distribution aligns with expected patterns, and importantly, there's evidence suggesting a connection between galaxy evolution and surrounding environmental factors, which must be considered.

This research proposes the establishment of a comprehensive database that will facilitate data sharing among climate scientists, enabling improved collaboration. Currently, over 1.5 million climate-related datasets are in circulation, but they are not effectively utilized due to the absence of interoperable interfaces. To address this issue, we suggest standardizing the climate datasets using a unified protocol known as CF Convention, which will enable their integration into the database. We also introduce a user-friendly interface called ClimaSearch, which will allow users to easily locate and access the climate data within our proposed repository.

Domain adaptation has long been a concern in NLP due to models trained on specific domain data struggling to perform well in other contexts. This problem is particularly acute in medical NLP, where models trained on hospital data often fail to generalize to new hospital settings. This research tackles this challenge by focusing on symptom event extraction across four distinct medical institutions, where data from three of them were used to train models and all four were used for evaluation. To address the issue, a new method called Symptom Extrapolation with Randomized overlook (SYRO) has been developed, which randomly excludes certain words during training, effectively simulating unseen symptoms and improving model adaptability. SYRO, combined with two other observation techniques, outperformed models without these methods in both supervised and self-supervised learning scenarios, with a significant improvement of 3-5% in F1 scores.

In the past decade, research into autonomous vehicles has gained significant momentum, driven by the potential to make driving safer and more efficient. However, human drivers face challenges in handling complex and unpredictable situations, such as navigating through crowded areas, adhering to traffic rules, and considering environmental and legal constraints. To address this, we propose a novel Deep Reinforcement Learning model that enables agents to learn optimal policies for autonomous driving, taking into account a set of fundamental rules for safe and efficient operation.

A promising approach for energy-efficient image classification in edge devices is the integration of spiking neural networks, which mimic the behavior of human brain cells.  The SNN model is versatile and can be trained using various methods, including backpropagation.  However, traditional conversion of trained CNN models to SNNs, which often involves replacing neurons with multiple spike generators, consumes excessive energy.  We have identified an alternative method, which involves using the Bernoulli distribution to train CNN models and directly mapping them to SNN models, resulting in significantly reduced energy consumption.  We have now expanded upon this discovery by proving it works for ResNet models as well, and also expanded our evaluation to include additional frameworks and datasets beyond ImageNet.  We have also made corrections to our original paper by addressing issues regarding data normalization and spike timing.

In this research, we investigate the properties of Strange Quark Matter (SQM) at high temperatures under the influence of temperature and isotropic nuclear matter. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of finite temperature and magnetic fields on the phase structure of SQM, and we examine the effect of these factors on the mass and radius of Neutron Stars.

High-performance computing clusters typically utilize volunteer computing to enhance their computational power by leveraging unutilized resources from users' personal devices. However, the individual computing resources they target are often compromised by user privacy concerns and anti-mining measures. We introduce Pando, a high-speed, distributed computing framework that enables individuals to participate in volunteer computing directly from their web browsers using a secure and privacy-preserving mechanism. Our solution effectively bypasses common detection methods allowing mining operations to proceed anonymously, and is demonstrated to have a negligible impact on browser and device performance. Furthermore, the security of Pando is rigorously validated through a formal proof of its security properties.

R.M. Snyman and N. MacLeod presented a novel class of eigenvalue problems that blend nonlinear elements with traditional eigenvalue problems. This category includes various practical applications in the areas of continuum mechanics, quantum physics, and optical engineering. The authors propose an innovative procedure for estimating nonlinear eigenvalues using the framework of minimal rational interpolation, with additional numerical techniques to enhance its performance. This estimation procedure can be executed in two variations: one that considers all previously computed spectral information and another limited to only the most recently obtained spectrum. The algorithm initially obtains a standard eigenvalue spectrum through an applied system, after which it iteratively incorporates each newly acquired spectrum, updating the interpolation model and corresponding approximation. The method was thoroughly tested against several benchmark problems and compared with an established estimation procedure in quantum physics known as the genetic algorithm.

The concept of intermediate beta-transformations, introduced by Hirst and Kemp in 2014, has been shown to have equivalent definitions by Kamae, Quere and Solomyak. One of their main findings involved the relationship between intermediate beta-transformations and avaricious beta-transformations, which have a specific property that excludes certain digit sequences. Although the proofs from Hirst-Kemp and Kamae-Quere-Solomyak relied heavily on each other, there's a missing detail in their argument that needs to be addressed. This note fills in the omission by providing a direct proof of a key lemma from Hirst-Kemp's work, which establishes that for any given intermediate transformation, there exists a highest base beta transformation that results in the same expansion for any number less than one, while also ensuring that the digit '0' is never included in the expansion of that number.

Lattice simulations of $QCD$ with fermions in a fundamental representation were studied using the 2d/3d Schwinger model to gain a clearer understanding of non-perturbative phenomena, particularly confinement and breaking of symmetries. By analyzing the static quark potential and Wilson loop, evidence of confinement, characterized by strings, was found. Further investigation into the 3d model revealed the presence of strings at low momentum. Additionally, studies of the 2d model involving different gauge groups and numbers of flavors, as well as lattice representations of the 3d model, confirmed the existence of strings. Finally, tests of various representations of the global symmetry group, including the use of the center symmetry, confirmed the signs of disruption of the symmetry.

Machine learning models like Random Forests and Adaboost, which are ensemble methods, have been largely overlooked for making predictions despite their exceptional accuracy in handling complex datasets. To address this issue, we've developed an after-the-fact explanation model, which is able to provide clear and accurate explanations for the black-box decisions made by these algorithms. Our approach, called DAG (Disentangled Attribution Graph), provides explanations that are not only more granular and accurate but also provide a more straightforward understanding of the model's behavior. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of our method on synthetic and real-world data, showing that it provides more accurate and clear explanations.

In scenarios where confidentiality is paramount, entities such as hospitals, financial institutions, and government bodies face challenges when attempting to collaborate on projects, such as joint research or data analysis, due to the presence of sensitive information. One potential solution, federated learning, relies on an untrusted central server, which compromises both collaboration and security. This paper proposes an innovative approach called federated training across execution environments, or Flatee, a collaborative framework that leverages trusted execution environments and their respective roots of trust to facilitate secure and private collaboration, even when the underlying infrastructure is untrusted. Flatee enables participants to run and train complex models, such as neural networks, within isolated environments, which are then securely verified and distributed, all without exposing any data to the central server. Experimental results demonstrate that Flatee achieves robust security and privacy, even in the face of sophisticated attacks, while also incurring minimal overhead in terms of latency and communication costs, making it a viable solution for real-world applications.

Ensuring the reliability of safety-critical systems relies heavily on precise timing predictions, which is particularly challenging with the proliferation of diverse processor options and the shift towards minimalistic, energy-efficient designs known as 'Small Footprint Embedded Systems'. Under these specific architectural conditions, standard high-level programming languages like C fail to deliver accurate timing predictions, necessitating a more sophisticated approach. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative methodology for automated operator timing analysis, tailored specifically to systems with a small footprint. This approach involves assigning timing properties to individual operators within a high-level timing diagram language, which can then be used to generate reliable timing predictions for complex algorithms. Our methodology is fully automated, user-friendly, and requires no specialized expertise, making it a practical solution for embedded system designers. To validate its efficacy, we carry out a thorough case study, comparing our approach with existing techniques and evaluating its benefits in a range of real-world applications.

One of the key challenges in deploying containerized applications is the performance degradation resulting from time-sharing mechanisms. This issue is particularly pronounced in calls between containers, which are often slowed down by the overhead of time-sharing. This paper introduces Timeloops, a cutting-edge technique that automatically detects ASs affected by time-sharing overhead and adjusts the scheduling of containerized applications to minimize delays. By using a unique time-based scheduling mechanism, Timeloops can mitigate the negative impact of time-sharing and improve the overall performance of inter-container calls. Our experimental results demonstrate that Timeloops can reduce the time-sharing-induced delay by up to 5.6 times, while also providing better quality of service and more predictable latency for inter-container communication.

This research examines Riemannian variants of perceptron algorithms on a commodity space form, a type of manifold with constant curvature. We demonstrate that these alternatives maintain linear classification abilities while retaining connections to traditional perceptron methods through specific convergence rates. The findings are further validated by presenting numerical results that compare the different classifiers in various scenarios.

This work presents a straightforward, illustrative model predictive control approach 
for determining the optimal operating parameters in a process with control delays. 
We compare two strategies: one that re-optimizes parameters in real-time and another 
that adjusts parameters only when delays exceed a specified threshold. Through a 
simple chemical reactor with multiple production goals, we show that both methods 
can effectively determine the optimal set of parameters, but only the adaptive approach 
consistently produces high-quality results. Furthermore, we examine the impact of 
prediction horizon length on simulation outcomes and provide a basis for selecting 
appropriate parameters.

This work bridges gaps in the theorems surrounding the asymptotic behavior of greedy learning algorithms, such as online and batch least-squares, when applied to non-stationary data streams, by drawing on insights from compressed regression models. A range of online and batch algorithms have been developed and demonstrated to converge at a rate of $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ and achieve an $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ generalization error of $\tilde{O}(k/T)^{1/2}$ and $\tilde{O}((k/t_t) \log(T/t_t))$, where $T$ is the total time steps, $k$ is the number of parameters, and $t_t$ is the time when the $k$th parameter is introduced. Our research expands on the existing compression theorems for regression, by introducing a class of compressed estimators for general non-stationary data, and introduces compressed variants of both the least-squares algorithm and gradient descent. These models have the potential to significantly reduce the communication cost between server and clients in a variety of applications, and our analysis quantifies the trade-off between their performance and the number of communication rounds, leading to potentially lower costs of interaction.

This study examines how competition and colonization influence species interactions, using a cellular automaton-based model of two competing species on a lattice. The authors analyze the effect of a competition-colonization trade-off, in which species with high colonization abilities have low competition abilities and vice versa. They find that this trade-off can lead to the elimination of one species through a complex process, or allow for the coexistence of both species in a patterned distribution. Numerical simulations reveal that the colonization and competition parameters determine whether species coexist in uniform numbers, eliminate one another, or allow for a stable two-species system. However, further analysis reveals that the uniform coexistence is unstable, leading to spontaneous formation of distinct species domains.

We show that in abelian quantum double models, regions with non-trivial topology or non-trivial homotopy can be associated with distinct von Neumann algebras. We compute equivalence functors for algebras in regions topologically equivalent and establish that any two algebras in regionally topologically equivalent areas have fully faithful morphisms between them. Furthermore, we construct a category from these algebras, with equivalence functors as morphisms, and demonstrate that this category is equivalent to the category of endofunctors on the Doplicher-Holger-Napoli category.

The couple between photons, magnons, and phonons was studied in a cavity magnomechanical system with a feedback loop using the driving field. Based on this setup, a feedback circuit was implemented to enhance the physical entanglement of the system. We found that the interplay between magnon-photon, magnon-phonon, and photon-phonon interactions gives rise to various forms of entanglement. Furthermore, the reflection signal also exhibits correlation with the system's entanglement. The introduction of the feedback circuit not only preserves but also improves upon these entanglement states, with the strength measured by the logarithmic negativity value. The extent of this enhancement is influenced by the coupling strengths between magnons, photons, and phonons, as well as the detuning between the driving field and magnon frequency.

We've compiled one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for all color and kinematic factors in A-D type theories, applying a standard regularization method. This is in continuation of previous work on QCD at one-loop. The compiled operators were then used to derive the one-loop matrix elements for a specific process, and it was found that these matrix elements have consistent singularities when certain particles become collinear, matching predicted patterns. Specifically, we calculated these matrix elements for processes involving four massless particles and up to eight loops.

In one-dimensional local rings, it's shown that the completion of the ring's formal power series can be approximated by a sequence of increasingly better subrings, which also cannot be approximated in a certain way from more complex rings, relating to a key mathematical concept known as Neron Desingularization.

Historical research in Indonesia is hindered by a lack of primary source accessibility, a problem exacerbated by local language barriers. This study aims to bridge this gap by identifying and translating key terms related to Indonesian sundials, a crucial navigation tool in pre-modern Southeast Asia. By examining historical documents, we've recovered and restored a forgotten tradition of recording sundial data, a method once used by Indonesian scholars to preserve historical timelines. This data collection approach, which combines astronomy and traditional timekeeping, provides a foundation for preserving cultural heritage through digital means.

This research paper introduces a novel coexistence of D2D communications, exploring how it can leverage both energy and data transfer capabilities. To achieve this, a new framework, the Intellect Reflecting Surface-Aided Integrated Information and Energy Networking (IRS-IEN) framework, is developed. This framework enables a D2D transmitter to simultaneously transmit data and energy to a nearby D2D user and a storage device, while also utilizing the IRS to optimize signal strength. By formulating a non-convex optimization problem, the study seeks to maximize the energy efficiency of the D2D communication, taking into account the efficiency of energy storage and backhaul connectivity. This problem is then broken down into two sub-problems, which are solved using techniques such as difference of convex functions and the Block Coordinate Descent method. The results demonstrate that the proposed solution converges quickly and outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency.

Researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands have developed a novel, cost-effective, and open-source system for 2D flow visualization utilizing a Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) technique. In this work, we outline a procedure to remotely operate a single-point LDV instrument, demonstrating how to position the detection volume and align the laser beams via a optical bench setup with a retroflector. Additionally, we provide a thorough explanation of the necessary steps to configure this setup for accurate flow velocity measurements.

The concept of first-order spectra is introduced, then explored specifically when a formula's truth depends on its inverse function being non-negative and bounded. This investigation specifically focuses on logical systems that include a relationship between elements that can be reversed, such as those with addition and multiplication operations.

A novel approach to correcting wave distortions in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) involves the use of programmable phase discs, in contrast to conventional methods that modify static optical components. We present an analysis of the theoretical capabilities of these phase discs as an aberration corrector, highlighting their advantages over traditional approaches. Furthermore, the phase discs' potential to simplify the process of aberration tuning is a notable benefit. Our research also encompasses evaluating their effectiveness in restoring phase contrast and their potential to correct the astigmatism-induced image shift.

This note aims to address certain mathematical calculations related to 
calculation surfaces, particularlyassessing the conditions for their existence. 
It seeks to clarify the concepts of calculation and assessment as well as 
establish criteria for theCalculation surface's appearance.

We derive an equation for a matrix, enabling the calculation of unique path counts from the origin to any point in a given number of steps while maintaining the same coordinates. This method is demonstrated through various applications, such as the mapping of points with the same distance from the origin in the曼哈顿 norm in the integer grid $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the classification of labeled partial permutations by their sign, and the computation of walk counts on the Cayley graph of the symmetric group $S_n$. The general formula obtained from these examples will likely have broader applications in combinatorics.

This research delves into the underlying geometry of a specific black hole model, investigating how its non-trivial structure can be represented within the expanded global spacetime framework. By doing so, we establish that this and other black hole models originate from a singular, compact Euclidean 2-torus space, and we further demonstrate that, in the expanded framework, these models exhibit distinct event horizons, thereby eliminating the Cauchy horizon. Building on this, we calculate the quasinormal modes for these black holes, and our findings align with previously published data, offering valuable insights into the gravitational wave signatures that may be detectable by observatories like LIGO and Virgo.

We've developed a semi-analytical model for describing interactions within doped graphene at finite temperatures.
This model is based on a non-retarded, temperature-dependent screened Coulomb potential.
The creation operators within this model adhere to exact equations of motion that incorporate
temperature effects and dynamic, temperature-dependent interactions.
Using this model, we calculated the quasi-particle energy and found that it aligns closely with
recent experimental data on graphene specific heat at high temperatures.
Additionally, our approach yielded an analytical expression for the thermal contribution to the specific heat,
which demonstrates agreement with numerical results from lattice simulations across all temperature ranges.
Our approach also enables precise determination of the quasi-particle mass and quasi-particle scattering rates.
These quantities are derived by matching our theoretical heat capacity to experimental data.
Our analysis reveals that the heat capacity is dominated by inter-band transitions beyond a certain temperature.
Our findings are consistent with those of a related theoretical study.

We introduce a novel method for enhancing context-aware speech capabilities, 
overcoming a key limitation of current synthesis techniques. The masking approach 
involve embedding placeholders, or'masks', into a reference text to temporarily 
suppress relevant segments during the parameter generation process. These segments 
are then reintegrated using a subsequent model that utilizes unmasked text to 
refine the desired parameters. Our framework combines two complementary modules, 
consisting of a mask learning component and a flow-based synthesis component. By 
separating these tasks and leveraging diverse training inputs, the two modules can 
be highly optimized and achieve superior performance. Our results demonstrate 
that the system is not only able to produce a wider range of speech sounds than 
previously possible, but also exhibits enhanced flexibility and adaptability.

The effectiveness of visual representations in supporting downstream tasks is widely acknowledged, yet its connection to coherent semantic understanding is less so. This study proposes that projection fields play a crucial role in enabling complex reasoning capabilities. We introduce SP4, a novel framework that projects 2D inputs into a latent space, where semantically meaningful projections emerge, facilitating accurate prediction. By leveraging this latent space, SP4 achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging image prediction datasets, including the WaterRipple, Plant, and Bubble datasets, outperforming the current benchmarks.

Recent studies have shown that traditional optimization methods can be easily exploited by attackers, leading to significant vulnerabilities in machine learning models. This has sparked a growing interest in research concerning the security and reliability of machine learning classifiers. While previous works focused on both white-box and black-box attacks using reference models, there has been a lack of exploration into assaults that mimic the capabilities of a malicious system administrator. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a new generative framework that enables two parties to collaborate in launching two types of collaborative attacks: one where the attacker modifies a single input, and another that allows multiple attackers to target a single input. We evaluate the effectiveness of these attacks and demonstrate their superiority in real-world scenarios, particularly when compared to existing black-box attack methods.

Climate change, a persistent issue for over three decades, has seen the spread of false information about the topic outpace legitimate scientific data. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the realm of climate communication, where a significant number of individuals, including a large portion of Twitter users, do not believe in the human-caused climate crisis. To better understand the root causes of this belief gap, this study examines the social media narratives surrounding four prevalent conspiracy theories – false climate data, altered time zones, climate simulation, and manipulated images – and their effect on shaping public perception of the climate crisis. By analyzing over 1.5 million individual tweets from more than 10,000 accounts, the research identifies key characteristics of accounts that propagate conspiracy theories, including their level of connectivity and the rate at which they propagate these narratives. Furthermore, the study reveals that conspiracy theories are often amplified by legitimate news outlets, and their effect varies depending on the type of platform and the frequency of exposure.

A study of shadow matter production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV is conducted using data from the CMS experiment at the LHC. The analysis, based on a cumulative 137 fb^-1 of recorded events, involves searching for uncommon top quark patterns. The investigation focuses on two distinct scenarios: one where a top quark and another signatureless entity are produced together, and another where two top quarks are created alongside two signatureless entities. The data obtained in the first scenario are consistent with background expectations and do not yield a statistically significant result for the existence of shadow matter, leading to the determination of a 95% confidence level upper limit on the cross-section of the relevant process. Additionally, in scenarios involving new physics at various energy scales, the findings can be interpreted in terms of equivalent standard model production, leading to constraints on the involved energy levels. The data also do not show a statistically significant discrepancy from background predictions in the second scenario, yielding a 95% confidence level upper limit on the cross-section of the relevant process. Furthermore, the data can be interpreted in terms of new physics at specific energy levels.

In an n-triangulated category triangled by橙色 S., which has finite dimensional Hom spaces, we establish as Lemma 1 that any object with zero i-th suspension is isomorphic to the zero object. Further, it's assumed in Theorem 2 that for any pair of objects in C, the direct sum of the cohomology groups modulo 848940 has a non-zero value. Based on this assumption, we prove in Corollary 3 that the category has a serried category structure. Building on this foundation, we establish the existence of a non-zero approximate identity in 848940-dimensional vector spaces as Proposition 4. Using this identity, we prove in Theorem 5 the existence of a non-exact long exact sequence in C that is associated with any non-unique morphism. Finally, based on the existence of this approximate identity, we define in Theorem 6 the notion of a non-unique left (resp. right) approximate identity for any non-exact long exact sequence in C.

Researchers often want to understand the long-term effects of fields of study on a person's earnings after graduation.  This goal is complicated by the fact that fields of study can be influenced by a person's innate abilities and also affect their skills in the workplace.  To address this challenge, the study employs a two-step approach.  First, it uses data on a person's grades in high school to predict their choice of field of study, and then examines the return on investment for each field.  Second, the study corrects for potential biases in this prediction by accounting for variations in the difficulty of fields and differences in high school course offerings across schools.  This method provides a more accurate estimate of the true earnings potential for fields of study.

Recent experiments using $J/\psi$-decay products in bubble-chamber studies have demonstrated that super $J/\psi$ decays produce a 100-fold increase in low-energy slow antiparticles compared to normal $J/\psi$ decays, particularly antineutrons and $\Lambda$ particles. These new energy sources will enable unprecedented access to low-energy $\bar{n}$-$n$ interactions, providing a highly precise measurement of the $\bar{d}$-$\bar{u}$ quark mass difference, which is predicted by the standard model to be the largest such difference, as well as allowing for the first-time observation of $\bar{n}$-$n$ charge exchange. Furthermore, experiments utilizing super $J/\psi$ decays have the potential to achieve sub-femtobar cross-section event production rates, leading to a thousand-fold improvement in the sensitivity of searching for the production of bound antinuclear matter states. Similarly, precise measurements of $\Lambda$ particle properties, such as the $\Lambda$-$\Sigma^{0}$ mass difference and weak interaction asymmetries, can be achieved with an order of magnitude greater precision.

If binary star formation begins with two protostars already connected, they would be surrounded by their own disks of material. These disks have the potential to further influence the binary's formation and evolution by pulling in more matter. Our goal is to understand how this additional matter affects the binary system when it forms. We used computer simulations to model this process and found that the inner binary system tends to gain mass at a steady rate of about 0.0000004 units of mass per time, which is consistent across different conditions. This speed is actually a bit slower than expected based on theoretical predictions. When more material falls into the system, it often ends up being evenly split between the inner binary and outer disk, which could have implications for the binary system's final state.

The consideration of the Universe as a finite system of interacting elements has been the subject of study in cosmology. Employing the concept of renormalization group, this study demonstrates that any universe composed of cells with the property of translational symmetry will inevitably exhibit a flat spacetime.

A new two-stage approach to image segmentation is proposed. Initially, a minimum-chief energy model with variable coefficients was developed. Then, an optimized numerical method was implemented to partition images into diverse regions, minimizing the energy model. Next, a unified framework for image enhancement and image segmentation was created. This framework employed a curvature-type partial differential equation to define region boundaries, with the L1 operator used to preserve partial details and edges. Lastly, the numerical method was applied to solve this equation and was demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world images. The proposed method effectively produced images with clear backgrounds and detailed foregrounds.

Heavy objects rotating in certain particle theories can interact with ultra-light particles in a way that allows them to transfer energy, leading the objects to lose their spin and mass. This phenomenon, called superradiance, is a promising way to use the speed changes seen in the speed of light from distant galaxies to narrow down the possible weights of these ultra-light particles. Researchers have now expanded on previous studies by taking into account how these galaxies form and evolve, and how light passes through space, and have found that the range of possible weights is much larger than previously thought. They have also discovered that considering how ultra-light particles change as they travel through space, and the properties of space itself, can further expand this range. They have also found that taking into account how galaxies move and the properties of space, can lead to a much larger range of possible weights for the ultra-light particles.

The open-source neuroscientific simulator Brian has been widely used for modeling various neuron types and connection rules. In contrast, the open-source neuromorphic processor Loihi, designed for efficient implementation of spiking neural networks, is not easily modeled using conventional code. Developing direct hardware code for the multi-core system of Loihi is a complex task. To address this challenge, we created an emulator for the Loiho processor within a Brian simulation, which we call Brian2Loihi. This emulator allows modeling PRC neurons and STDP synapses on hardware identical to the one in Loihi.

The characteristics of a noisy emission source were successfully tracked in 3D across various wavelengths, marking a first, using SDO/AIA data. This was achieved by applying an advanced algorithm, known as the Almaden tomographic source surface forward fit (ATS3SFF), to a case of a microflare. This particular event, occurring at a specific coordinate, exhibited a significant increase in brightness, which was observed at multiple wavelengths, including 13.1, 299, and 211 nm. This brightening was found to be linked to a change in the source's height, a drop in its size, and a shift in its location. These evolutionary patterns were found to be consistent across the observed wavelengths, suggesting that the flaring event affected plasma at different heights. This study highlights the value of applying ATS3SFF to solar flares and provides a new method for understanding the complex behavior of these dynamic phenomena.

Researchers have created a new, two-dimensional integrated magnetic optical trap that allows for efficient manipulation of atoms in a confined space without requiring additional-dimensional room. This innovation has implications for developing compact atom chips and systems for optically controlling atoms. We have successfully realized this type of trap using planar integrated magnets and optically trapped atoms, followed by a detailed investigation of its characteristics. Given its functionality, this new approach can be applied to various optically trapping methods, offering advantages over traditional methods.

Our research examines how a cluster of particles falls towards a non-rotating black hole when initially confined within a specified finite area of space. The initial setup features particles at rest within this volume and we analyze the temporal evolution of the system's phase space density as well as key properties such as the mass falling into the black hole over time and particles escaping to infinity. The study reveals that if there are no particles with non-zero angular momentum, all particles eventually escape to infinity. However, if some particles possess non-zero angular momentum, they can be captured by the black hole. The system's long-term behavior is characterized by the development of caustics, which are intricate structures with self-similar patterns. The research also reveals that in certain regimes, a power-law relationship exists between the mass falling into the black hole over time and time itself.

This paper focuses on how an excited atom behaves when near a narrow rectangular mirror, specifically analyzing the situation where the atom moves away from its initial excitation point. The investigation involves calculating and比较 the differences in the different decay pathways and average emission times caused by the atom's motion to different scenarios whether it is stationary or moving. Additionally, the study examines how directional changes in the atom's emitted light are affected by its movement in relation to various polarisation patterns.

A comprehensive study of the region surrounding Westerlund 2 has been conducted, yielding a detailed color-magnitude diagram and essential information about the area's stellar population. Researchers discovered numerous giant stars, including some exceptionally luminous examples, and obtained spectra for many of them. These findings indicate that many of the giant stars are located outside Westerlund 2 itself, and that the area contains numerous blue and red giant stars with varying characteristics. Importantly, the study reveals that many of the giant stars exhibit a lack of H and He absorption lines, and that some red giant stars exhibit unique metal absorption patterns. Ultimately, these findings provide valuable insights into the stellar evolution processes occurring in this fascinating cluster and surrounding region.

This study focuses on finding grounded solutions to the problem of minimizing functions, $u$, within the space $H^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ under the constraint of being in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^2)$. These solutions are related to a specific type of nonlocal biharmonic equation with a critically sized nonlinear term, featuring interaction within an exponential ground state. We have established the existence and distinct characteristics of these solutions. Additionally, we observed the existence of multiple solutions in specific scenarios.

Historical documents, although rich in information, are often difficult to read due to deterioration, making full text recognition (TR) tasks more challenging. While existing methods primarily focus on restoring degraded text to improve machine readability, there's a lack of research aimed at enhancing visual quality for a better reading experience. This paper introduces a multi-task adversarial network that not only restores degraded handwritten documents but also improves their visual quality through an adversarial process. This approach outperforms existing methods in restoration and surpasses well-established image synthesis methods on standard metrics, while also producing visually sharper and more realistic results as confirmed by human evaluation.

The reliance on physical documents like invoices and IDs creates storage and organization challenges, as well as the issue of wasted space. One possible solution is to utilize ID card extraction, but the process is often hindered by language barriers and image quality issues. To address these problems, a solution was developed to extract data from Indonesian identity cards, utilizing Keras-TensorFlow for learning and OpenCV for image enhancement. The extraction process is further refined using Keras and BERT language models. The proposed method's accuracy is KPI-driven, focusing on specific error rates. The results show that the proposed approach successfully extracts data with high accuracy rates of 96.75% for name, NIK, and place of birth.

In vehicular networks based on IEEE 802.11p standard, the mobility of vehicles significantly degrades channel estimation accuracy, leading to errors. To mitigate this issue, we propose a method utilizing an LSTMs autoencoder to enhance channel estimation accuracy. The training of this model is achieved using a limited number of pilots, allowing it to be trained offline. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses the IEEE 802.11p standard and other existing techniques in terms of accuracy.

Astronomers are increasingly utilizing visual observations to gather data, given their cost-effectiveness and ease of collection. Historically, image colorization has aided scientists, but current cost reductions in technology now allow it to supplement other observation methods, such as black-and-white images taken with charge-coupled devices. We present a cost-efficient deep learning-based image colorization system compatible with common CCD devices, allowing obtained images to be colorized, enhanced, and de-noised. This system uses a modified Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that outperforms conventional image colorization methods, providing quicker processing and higher-quality results. Our approach features two-stage processing: initially, a de-noising module is employed, followed by colorization, resulting in more accurate color representation and reduced computational expenses by avoiding the use of a single module. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, showing that this system can significantly reduce costs for obtaining color data.

Optimizing sub-optimal solutions in complex systems is a significant challenge due to numerous interdependent variables. The drop-out of high-frequency components in fast-evolving systems can lead to overfitting, making it difficult to accurately predict the full system. Existing methods for adjusting complex systems rely on gradient-based methods, which are often inefficient and prone to local optima. An alternative, more efficient method for reconfiguring fast-evolving complex systems is needed. We propose a novel, efficient approach using universal estimation to optimize the parameters of a neural network without relying on gradients. Our method exploits the rapid convergence of SVD and minimizes the impact of high-frequency data on under-determined sub-matrices by iteratively removing the largest singular value from the matrix. Our results show that our method outperforms standard back-propagation in terms of convergence speed and generalization ability.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRC) was established in 2007 to support and promote the development of career researchers within the particle and nuclear physics community.  Comprising representatives from experimentalists, theorists, and career development professionals, the committee actively engages in providing a platform for career researchers to share experiences and seek assistance.  During its tenure from January 2021 to December 2022, the ECRC committee organized workshops, published career guidance material, and coordinated career support initiatives alongside the parent committee.

Due to their strong nonreciprocity and compact size, photonic crystal slabs are well-suited for creating nonreciprocal optical devices. However, they are limited in generating line waves due to low quality factors and complex fabrication processes. A new approach uses a dual metastructure to generate line waves from a feed wave with high efficiency and simplicity. The first layer consists of magnetic resonators, while the Faraday film in the second layer converts this wave into line waves with a specific frequency. This structure only produces line waves when the input frequency meets a precise condition. A line wave is formed as a result of the interaction between the two layers, and it can only form at a specific frequency. The research shows that the line wave can be excited with a 70% efficiency when there is no gap between the layers, and with 40% efficiency when there is a nanometer gap. Furthermore, adding a nanometer gap allows the generated line wave to be tunable.

In the field of multi-agent learning, researchers have made significant strides, particularly in complex cooperative tasks. However, this work has not yet been effectively translated into real-world applications, especially involving large-scale human-robot collaborations. Our team's experience building a cognitive AI framework for a 2.5-meter bridge construction task underscores the need for new approaches. We identify two key challenges: making the cognitive AI system accessible to a broad audience and allowing for easy integration of new learning capabilities. We propose a novel, modular architecture based on learning from demonstration, leveraging actionable traits and a knowledge graph. This approach has enabled our team to learn and adapt the cognitive AI system to real-world collaborative tasks, even with limited examples.

Estimation of variation measures like the mean absolute deviation (MAD) around the mean has gained significant interest in recent years, largely due to the realization that median-based estimation methods yield more robust results. However, it is well-established that standard unbiased MAD estimators are biased, particularly in cases with symmetric distributions where they exhibit negative bias. In this study, we explore methods to reduce this bias in both finite and large sample contexts, utilizing correction factors that depend on the underlying distribution. Our research also compares several bias-reduced estimators through simulations and empirical examples to determine their effectiveness.

A critical task in natural language processing, specifically in extracting information from text, involves recognizing and categorizing the connection between two entities within a given sentence, referred to as relation extraction. This current research aims to bridge the gap between two prominent artificial intelligence subfields: knowledge graph link prediction and relation extraction by treating the missing connections between entities in a graph as sentences to analyze. This approach enables an AI system to anticipate which additional connections between entities are likely to occur and uses this prediction to refine its understanding of a query, thereby enhancing its ability to accurately identify a entity's relationship with another.

A comprehensive analysis of polarization and transverse momentum broadening of $\Psi$ and $J/\Psi$ in an $N$-dimensional plasma is conducted, with a focus on the anisotropy of momentum and quasi-particle Debye mass, and a higher-order transport equation in a anisotropic frame. An anisotropic quasi-particle density matrix formalism in the anisotropic frame is formulated in the anisotropic frame, with the help of an $N$-dimensional operator. An anisotropic quasi-particle density matrix in the anisotropic frame, with a first-order and higher-order transport equation, is formulated in the anisotropic frame, and it is observed that with the increase of anisotropy parameter and chemical potential, there is a significant change in polarization and broadening of polarization.

Our investigation of Tb3RuO7, a member of the 4d transition metal pyrochlore family, reveals a complex magnetic arrangement at low temperatures, characterized by alternating bonds in its spin-3/2 Ru chains. Neutron diffraction experiments show that in the range of 0.35-2 K, the system exhibits a partially disordered state, and this partially disordered state undergoes a transition into a spiral state below 0.35 K, with a periodic length of approximately 10-12 unit cells. Notably, this periodic length is comparable to that of Tb3Ox pyrochlore analogs, which typically exhibit spiral states with periodic lengths of 6-8 unit cells. Furthermore, the presence of an internal magnetic field oriented perpendicular to the Ru chains, and the discovery of a magnetic field with opposite polarity in the Tb sublattice, are new findings that distinguish this material from its pyrochlore analogs.

In the field of computer vision, feature extraction and text generation, recurrences are commonly used but suffer from limited capacity and convergence issues. A solution lies in representing sequences functionally, albeit such representations are complex and challenging to train. For health care applications, it's essential for generated features to be easily understood by humans, as they are ultimately used for diagnosis. A new framework for learning local functions to represent temporal or spatially structured data is presented, which decomposes learned functions into interpretable components, such as activations, weights, and biases. A novel architecture called MODAR enables the composition and modulation of these components in an attention-based manner, resulting in high-quality, human-interpretable features. Through extensive experiments and ablation studies, the framework is shown to outperform previous approaches in multiple baselines and tasks, while also allowing for the analysis of its computational and functional structure.

Achieving fair treatment decisions across various demographic groups is a significant challenge in both research and practical applications. Current approaches typically rely on semi-supervised methods that utilize paired data from multiple groups to calculate parity metrics. However, these methods are impractical to implement due to the difficulty of collecting paired samples. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework called semi-generative modeling, which generates synthetic paired data based on group-specific marginal distributions. This approach enables the use of traditional equality-of-opportunity metrics in scenarios where paired data are unavailable. By combining element-wise Kullback-Leibler divergence minimization with GAN-style minimax optimization, semi-generative modeling ensures the accurate reconstruction of conditional distributions. Moreover, this method obviates the need for outcome mimicry, a common feature of GANs that can lead to mode collapse. We evaluate the efficacy of semi-generative modeling through extensive experiments using real-world datasets, including Adult, Bank, and Bank8, and demonstrate its superior performance in multiple dimensions.

Deep learning, particularly its representation layer, is a crucial component of AI, but it lacks a comprehensive theoretical understanding. We introduce a framework to explain the operation of deep learning models, drawing from representation learning and transferable function concepts. By analyzing this theory, we can gain insight into why certain models are highly effective and why they are able to perform tasks outside their initial training context. Our research further reveals the geometric properties of the representation space and its relationship to the model's functional behavior.

In 2009, Kowalski and Miličević identified patterns of local minima in the growth of the arithmetic function $\sigma(n)/dn$, where the notable grid local minima stood out. The pattern of these grid minima can be explained using the concepts of standard harmonic numbers and the natural logarithm of $n$, combined with specific corrections related to Mertens' theorems. Furthermore, the concept of replacing prime powers with factorial numbers offers a generalized approach to understanding this phenomenon. The study also establishes lower bounds for non-trivial grid minima and provides a framework for investigating higher-dimensional local minima patterns.

The substantial data generated by the Large Hadron Collider requires sophisticated analysis, and recent advancements in observables have been made using deep neural networks. However, their "black box" nature poses a challenge in understanding their contributions to the classification. To bridge this gap, we propose combining these novel features with traditional, physically-based variables. By applying the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation technique, we've been able to assess the relative importance of each feature. Our analysis, performed on a public dataset and a production dataset from ALFA and ATLAS experiments, reveals that a class of neural networks can outperform tree-based ensembles when paired with LRP and suitable reference patterns.

This study introduces a novel variation of r-linked Stirling numbers, termed degenerate r-linked Stirling numbers, and examines its properties through a unique degenerate identity. We also establish related mathematical expressions.

Researchers initially demonstrated that certain types of network organizations, specifically those based on格雷编码 and 顺序编码, inherently possess location symmetries that cause degenerate representations in graph theory.  In our work, we investigate how these various network organization types affect representation structure by defining new, more complex organizations that combine 单/双层结构 with 顺序编码 or 对称编码.  By merging group actions on vertex sets with network organization principles, we identify the core influence of symmetry on representation architecture, revealing that both local and global symmetries result in degenerate representations.  To address this issue, we define the concepts of irreducible and location-symmetric induced representations and establish novel network organization models that facilitate the creation of these representations.  Furthermore, we illustrate the relationships between the underlying group properties and the characteristics of the degenerate/irreducible representations, demonstrating that the inherent network symmetries can be directly linked to the type of representation induced by the graph's induced group action.

In this research, a specific class of vector fields, specifically certain Killing vectors, is identified. These vectors have the characteristic of generating rotations or translations, resulting in cyclic or linear motion respectively. Building on this finding, a general impulse operator utilizing these vectors is established and tested with various manifolds, including the sphere, torus, and Poincare surface. Furthermore, a theory is proposed regarding the creation of geodesic integral paths for these vectors when utilizing the identified impulse operator.

A crucial aspect of quantum many-body theory, known as the sign problem, poses a significant challenge in formulating physical systems. It arises due to the oscillation of wave function values between positive and negative, making it difficult to perform accurate Monte Carlo simulations. This problem becomes more severe as the complexity of the system increases, ultimately making exact solutions unattainable. Recent advancements, such as using neural networks to model wave functions, have provided a more practical approach for approximating ground states. However, these methods are still hindered by sign fluctuations, which are especially prominent in quantum field theories. To address this issue, we propose integrating a complex number property into the network to prevent sign oscillations, thereby improving the efficiency of the simulation process, as demonstrated by successful experiments on the transverse field Hubbard model.

If new physics is linked to the Higgs field, the scale at which it occurs could be close to electroweak symmetry breaking. This paper explores a wide range of models where the fundamental components of a composite Higgs are light, nearly massless bosons, similar to chiral pions in low-energy QCD, and demonstrates how these models share common characteristics. These features include the Higgs acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, chiral Lagrangians utilizing effective theories, penguin diagrams inducing $\bar{B}_{s} \to \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decays that can be matched with experimental observations, and the possibility of the Higgs being produced through vector resonances vector boson fusion.

Research in the field of VR has long been driven by an interest in using the technology to mimic and study human perception. This goal is based on the premise that creating a simulated, artificial world that adheres to the rules of geometry, air perspective, and sound can induce the same perceptual changes that occur in the real world. Notably, the act of navigating through a virtual environment will always produce side effects, such as altered bodily sensations, regardless of the specific content of that environment.

To bridge the language disparity gap, numerous pre-trained language models have been developed. Despite improvements, translating text into a different language can still yield subpar translations. In this research, we aim to enhance the BigScience, pre-trained language model by incorporating additional languages beyond its original 10, to produce more accurate translations. First, we examine the effectiveness of pre-trained models on various tasks. Next, we explore zero-shot translation by testing Bilingual and Multilingual models on new languages without prior training. Subsequently, we fine-tune these models using diverse datasets and assess the performance of the resulting models. Finally, we conduct a comparative analysis of the modified models against existing state-of-the-art models to validate our approach.

Recent findings from the ALMA survey of star formation suggest that most binary systems are formed when a single, rotating cloud core splits, and core masses keep growing as they continue forming stars. This core fission process is an area of active research, and understanding how it works is essential for our knowledge of star formation.
