We introduce a novel class of ideals in ring theory called feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. A proper ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ meets our criteria if, for any ideals $A, B, C$ in the ring, the condition $ABC \subseteq I$ results in either the combination $(A \setminus I) \cup (B \setminus I)$ or $A \setminus I \cup IC \subseteq I$ or $AI \cup (B \setminus I) \subseteq I$. The 1-absorbing prime ideals represent a special case of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. The research also establishes a relationship between feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and $1$-absorbing primitive ideals. Furthermore, 1-absorbing prime ideals exhibit a strong connection with feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Research on feebly $1$-primitive ideals and feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals is initiated.

We have developed a method to identify the $\rho$ meson in three-body B meson decays by utilizing information about the hadrons produced in the recoil B meson's decay. This technique was applied to a dataset collected by the Belle II detector, containing $3.0 \times 10^{10}$ precisions, and was used to reconstruct the two-body decay process. Our results demonstrate an efficiency of reconstruction and allow for further analysis of the data.

As astronomers gather more information from the numerous telescopes and surveys being constructed, the task of combining and interpreting the vast data sets becomes increasingly complex.  A common approach is cross-correlation, which can be used to match spectra from different sources, but it often suffers from inaccuracies.  These errors can be attributed to several factors, including the need to reduce data from larger datasets, the need to focus on particular areas, and the need to reduce noise, all of which can be addressed using the same techniques used to improve the quality of images.  To overcome these limitations, we suggest the use of the high-throughput spectral multiplexing technology known as photonic spectrum slicing to improve the efficiency and accuracy of spectral cross-correlation methods.

A new approach for predicting adverse drug interactions is presented, utilizing a more accurate definition that considers how one medication affects the functionality of a second medication. The proposed model, a modification of Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), is a Relational ADAM (RDM) network that models medication pairs as a complete graph with 4 nodes representing individual atoms within the medications. A major limitation of current methods is their reliance on atom-level data, which fails to capture essential chemical properties. By employing a multi-node graph structure and aggregating node embeddings using attention-based methods, our framework better captures the essential characteristics of each medication. The proposed model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art methods in benchmarks and provided insight into the chemical properties involved in adverse drug interactions through node embedding analysis.

The quality of roads has a significant impact on the safety and mobility of pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists, as road hazards like uneven surfaces, potholes, and steep inclines can cause accidents and discomfort, as well as financial losses and vehicle damage. To address this, we have developed a system that uses a combination of computer vision and machine learning to automatically identify and detect road hazards, as well as quantify their severity levels, by utilizing high-resolution images and allowing for the inclusion of additional data such as road type and gradient. Our approach leverages a pre-trained deep learning model, which is then fine-tuned on a manually labeled dataset of road hazards, as well as being adaptable to new countries, as evidenced by our successful testing with a UK-based dataset following initial training with a South African one, with the results showing an 87% accuracy rate.

We're tackling the challenge of teaching an agent unfamiliar domain skills by leveraging expertise from another familiar domain. Unlike existing research that relies on knowledge transfer between similar domains, our approach focuses on less comparable domains and L2 skills that can't be directly observed. Since observing an agent perform unfamiliar actions is often impractical, we've developed a approach that L2 skills are learned from the agent's domain state trajectories, without needing visual input. Our approach and experiments demonstrate that our method can effectively train agents in both visual and non-visual domains using only visual data from a single source domain.

Three-dimensional population III protostar-accretion disk simulations are conducted to investigate the impact of magnetic field strength on disk fragmentation. We discovered that in domains with an atomic or molecular gas surface density greater than 100 g/cm^2, fragmentation occurs rapidly within as little as one orbital period, even at relatively mild temperatures of 80 K. This is in stark contrast to previous two-dimensional simulations, which showed fragmentation only in disks with gas surface densities exceeding 1000 g/cm^2. We attribute this to the enhanced population III magnetic field, which significantly amplifies torques that overcome thermal and centrifugal support, thereby facilitating disk fragmentation. This phenomenon is further exemplified by observations of brown dwarf formation from the Primordial Gas Cloud 0313-51, which features a initial gas surface density of 100 g/cm^2. This implies that the formation of sub-stellar objects may be facilitated in certain disk environments, offering an alternative to the conventional star formation process.

Machine learning and data mining techniques such as association rule mining have become integral components in multiple data processing and learning frameworks. The ever-growing number of theories and methods in this domain necessitates a unified approach to clarify foundational concepts and relationships between different techniques. This paper contributes to this goal by introducing a unified framework for association rule mining, based a lattice structure for knowledge bases and its homomorphisms. Through this abstract framework, we examine the properties of minimal bases and provide methods for identifying them, which can be applied to various finding algorithms.

This study examines how a random selection of individuals who were mandated to attend therapy after conviction differs from those who were not assigned to the therapy program. The analysis focuses on the characteristics of these groups and their outcomes in the criminal justice system. The results show that individuals assigned to the therapy program came from more disadvantaged backgrounds before their conviction. The study also reveals that the decision to assign individuals to the therapy program was influenced by their criminal history and risk assessment. The outcomes indicate that the therapy program has a significant impact on reducing recidivism and improving rearrest rates among participants. The analysis suggests that the therapy program may be an effective intervention for addressing underlying issues contributing to criminal behavior.

A new class of Apostol-Bernoulli generalized polynomials is defined and its properties, particularly its type, are investigated. Recurrence relationships for this new class are established. Various applications are given, along with the definition of special types of Apostol-Bernoulli generalized polynomials. Notably, their connection to existing polynomials is demonstrated.

Radio mapping is a well-established method for mapping the signal strength landscape, 
which is typically employed by wireless operators to identify high-interference areas.
Although drones have been used in specific scenarios, using them to map the strength landscape 
on a large scale has not been extensively explored. This paper presents a novel system that leverages
drones to efficiently collect a vast amount of data points in a short period of time. The proposed system
enables strong signals to be detected at high altitudes, thus increasing the data throughput. The radio map
generated using this system has been compared to one generated through a traditional pedestrian-based approach.

Identifying unusual patterns in industrial settings is a complex task.
A novel, unsupervised learning method is introduced for detecting anomalies
in continuous data streams. This approach utilizes hidden Markov models to
build a database of normal behavior and an evaluation system based on entropy
to identify deviations. The effectiveness of the proposed method is
demonstrated through simulation and real-world application on power generation
plant performance measurements.

This research proposes a comprehensive system for verifying unique individuals based on their audio-visual-thermal characteristics. Building upon existing studies on single-modal and multi-modal biometric authentication, this innovatively integrats depth estimation using the Thermal-IR and Visual spectra's NCC, enhancing the robustness of the authentication process even in the event of modality failures. System components are evaluated using established, publicly accessible datasets, with results demonstrating a notable accuracy rate of 99.75\% on the CASIA-FVDR dataset.

We present a method to improve the performance of sequence-to-sequence models with limited training data and reduced length, resulting in a significant decrease in error rates for automatic speech recognition and machine translation. The constraint leads to a model that is more informed about each training example, including hidden states that are not present in the original data. We increase the amount of training data by creating variations of the original samples through two methods - velocity, which generates slightly shifted translations, and length, which creates completely new sentences of increasing length. These variations are then added to the training set. The proposed approach does not require any adjustments to the original training data or models, making it applicable to both baseline and advanced models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique on multiple benchmarks, achieving a notable improvement in automatic speech recognition and machine translation with no additional data.

When evaluating the effectiveness of different sampling strategies, researchers often compare average parameters from different probability distributions of sample sizes. Assessing average parameters from these distributions can be challenging, particularly when dealing with mixture distributions of possible sample sizes. This paper presents a maximum likelihood approach for estimating parameters of distribution components within a mixture model. It then extends these estimates to calculate average parameters and their associated standard deviations, presenting two distinct scenarios for weighted and unweighted component distributions. The proposed method is illustrated through applications in sampling.

Achieving a balance between data protection and utility in machine learning is a significant challenge. To maintain data confidentiality, researchers have developed the concept of one-sided differential privacy, which offers a more relaxed framework for guaranteeing data privacy. This concept ensures that an adversary cannot infer specific information about individual data points. However, even within this relaxed framework, data privacy can be compromised if an adversary has prior knowledge about certain data characteristics. This study investigates data privacy breaches that occur despite one-sided differential mechanisms by leveraging existing prior knowledge about data characteristics. Based on this research, we have developed one-sided differential mechanisms capable of protecting information about characteristics commonly found in datasets. We have also created the Fuzzy Mechanism, which can provide both privacy and flexibility, allowing for the incorporation of data into models without compromising confidentiality.

The origin and development of protoplanetary disks are ongoing areas of research. We're able to study this process in greater detail with the help of the Atacama Major Planet Array (ALMA). We've used this facility to observe the disk of AS 209, a gas-rich T Tauri star located approximately 140 parsecs away. Data from ALMA's 0.3'-1.8' sized beams at CO J=2-1 and 3-2 wavelengths, with spatial resolutions of 0.22" and 0.16", respectively, reveal a significant CO emission gap in the inner disk. This structure is characterized by an exponential decline in CO emission outside the gap, with a full width at half maximum of 0.34", 0.27", and 0.20" for the p=1-0, p=2-1, and p=3-2 lines. The CO emission gap's full width at half maximum is 0.056", 0.047", and 0.040". Data from CO J=2-1 and 3-2 lines indicate that the dust ring lies within the CO gap's boundaries. This suggests a narrow dust ring surrounding a CO-rich gas disk. Data from CO J=2-1 and 3-2 lines suggest a dust ring with a full width at half maximum of 0.

An analysis of certain properties, such as fluorescence, often involves analyzing flash-startled emissions over time. This process typically relies on analyzing time-stamped photon data. Although analysis tools for flavyones have been developed, similar tools for studying other materials, like per- and polyfluorinated compounds (PFCs) and similar substances, have not been widely established. We have created a comprehensive software package to aid in starting such analyses. This package consists of a program, along with a related analysis module and an accompanying analysis manual. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this software package by applying it to a specific analysis of time-stamped data from the phosphorescent compound bis(triarylamine) oxide.

This paper considers a type of parabolic equation with a constrained control and limited state variables, in the context of mean field games. Under specific conditions, we demonstrate the presence of weak solutions, and moreover, we prove the uniqueness of these solutions when certain regulatory coefficients adhere to a strict linear constraint.

Recent high-precision data from the Gaia mission has enabled a groundbreaking approach to studying the disk of the Milky Way by analyzing individual star movements. Traditionally, the galaxy's structure was visualized through "stellar threads," but our new research utilizes Gaia's velocity data to create a 3D model of the galaxy's dynamics, effectively rendering these threads obsolete. Instead, we've developed a more accurate representation of the galaxy's evolution, incorporating the formation of star clusters and the movement of stars, providing valuable insights into the underlying processes at work.

Recent advancements in computer vision have enabled the development of sophisticated models capable of generating semantic images, but detecting differences between real and manipulated images remains a difficult task. Current methods are susceptible to manipulation techniques such as in-painting and in-coding, which can be bypassed by advanced algorithms. To address this issue, we propose Visual Identification for Counterfeit Detection with Transformers (VICTOR), a novel approach that leverages transformers and fashion-specific contrastive pre-training to accurately distinguish between real and manipulated images. By fine-tuning the transformer model and incorporating a fashion item classifier, VICTOR is able to identify even subtle differences between real and manipulated images, outperforming current state-of-the-art detection methods.

Recent years have seen a surge in the mathematical and physical investigation of quantum resource theories. This methodical approach involves formulating an algebraic framework for classifying quantum states, defining free states, free operations, and resource-related protocols. This standard procedure has been successfully applied to a diverse array of states, including coherent states, number states, and hybrid states. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive and accessible overview of the recent literature on the rigorous formulation of quantum resource theories, with a particular focus on the properties of nonclassical light.

One key challenge in deep neural network training is the difficult-to-interpret difference vector used as the update measure. This issue is particularly pronounced in distributed settings, where it's often used to track progress.以往的研究倾向于采用异步方法，在服务器端保持无约束的更新，而在服务器施加约束则会导致与客户端不同的优化路径，从而在服务器和客户端之间产生偏差。然而，我们观察到，即使异步执行，异步更新可以在一定步数之后达到稳定的状态，并且与同步方法相比，具有较好的收敛性能和结果。性能评估包括性能、收敛性和结果两个方面。

This study draws parallels between the classical operational calculus of Riemann-Liouville and the operational calculus within the Bessel-Macdonald space, utilizing a space of polynomial tempered distributions and functions, as well as a class of kernels with specific growth restrictions. We establish a connection between the four basic operations (addition, multiplication, differentiation, integration) and their corresponding Riesz-Dini sections, deriving expressions for polynomial tempered distributions and their associated functions. Furthermore, this research examines key properties, such as the associativity and distributivity, of the operation within the Bessel-Macdonald space.

A proposed criterion for the shadow dimension is evaluated in relation to recent findings by Arvanitakis et al. These findings suggest the existence of a new particle with the characteristics of the hypothetical dark matter candidate known as the axion-like particle. We propose that this new particle is part of a system that includes primordial black holes, which serve as a guide to the "Swampland" theory's constraints. These constraints include the absence of scale invariant classical potentials and massless particles, which are integral to the development of dark matter theories.

Research on the statistical behavior of molecular self-assembly has gained significant attention, focusing on the creation of ordered structures, known as self-assembled monolayers, which are found in both nature and technology. To understand the statistical properties of these structures, researchers have turned to the example of levitated soap films, or molecular soaps, due to their ease of observation and the ability to manipulate them. However, the comparison with 2D liquid drops, which exhibit well-understood ordered structures, has highlighted key differences in the creation of ordered structures, notably the absence of a Wenzel state in molecular soaps. To address the question of fracture in molecular soaps, researchers have employed the use of an external force to induce fractures and have found that the system behaves according to 2D liquid drop models, suggesting a potential approach to fabricate 2D ordered structures, or molecular lakes, through the use of confinement and external pressure.

In recent years, research has focused on improving the mobility of GaN. Although the mobility of GaN in high electron mobility transistors is not a major issue, its low mobility in oscillating gate transistors significantly hampers performance. To address this, a new concept called anisotropic strain was introduced to enhance mobility in specific directions. This technique, however, is difficult to implement. Our results show that aligning the crystallographic axes of GaN with ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ in a $\sqrt{2}\times \sqrt{2}$ structure allows for the application of anisotropic strain. This innovation enables the development of GaN channels in anisotropic strain field effect transistors, maximizing mobility in the direction of the current flow.

Achieving fully autonomous navigation in the dynamic and complex terrain of marine environments is a significant challenge, largely due to the high cost of collecting training data and modeling the environment's changing patterns. Our proposed method leverages long-term expense data collected from an autonomous robot to create a prior knowledge space, using active learning to select the most informative expense points for training. The environment's temporal variations are then learned through a gauge process model, using only a limited set of expense data. Our approach successfully reduces the number of required long expense samples, allowing for more efficient learning of an expense function, environment segmentation, and time-series expense prediction, as demonstrated by experimental results.

This study delves into complex isometric transformations, specifically focusing on isometric symmetries of meromorphically isothermal surfaces. These transformations include Darboux and Calapso, which we find exhibit significant relationships with the Gauss map and harmonic 1-forms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both transformations preserve key properties, such as isothermal parameters, isometry, and conformal properties. Interestingly, our research shows that both transformations can be expressed in relation to the Weierstrass data, which provides a consistent framework for understanding their connections to the respective isothermal parameters.

Nonparametric regression offers a flexible alternative to traditional regression by allowing for an arbitrary function relationship, thereby eliminating the need for specific parametric form assumptions. Nonetheless, when dealing with multivariate regressors or intricate functional dependencies, convergence at an optimal rate can pose significant challenges. This discussion focuses on various nonparametric estimation techniques, particularly those employing smoothing methods, and examines their pros and cons through illustrative examples in real data analysis.

This paper examines the $\lambda$-versions of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated identities, including the $\lambda$-versions of key properties such as the sum, sign alteration, recurrence relation, inverse, and differential equation.

The expanding volume of interconnected data has created a need to manage relationships between entities in various domains, a concept known as the Knowledge Graph (KG). With many potential missing connections between entities, researchers have developed frameworks for predicting future relationships, known as link prediction. While several methods considering temporal changes in relationships exist, many overlook the evolution of an entity's characteristics over time. Our study focuses on how incorporating a static framework, representing an entity's enduring properties, can enhance the predictive ability of traditional temporal methods, such as TransE, for forecasting time-based relationships, such as those found in the Facebook Places graph.

Cuntz-Krocker-Nakamura recently established that two finite graphs having isomorphic graph power series lead to shift-equivalent infinite graphs with locally finite structures. Consequently, the C*-algebras associated with Cuntz-Schmidt generators are naturally morita-equivalent. However, this conclusion does not hold for graphs that do not allow natural embeddings. Therefore, we develop a concept of robust shift equivalence that is more inclusive and then examine its implications in terms of natural and non-natural embeddings between graphs. Additionally, we provide a straightforward test to determine if two graphs are robustly shift equivalent and show that the robust equivalence classes consist of only finitely many graphs. This new idea of robust shift equivalence leads to a more general relationship between the graph's Laplacian matrix and the trace values of its powers.

In the quark-gluon plasma under influence of an intense magnetic field, the polarization of particles produced from heavy quark decay is altered as a result of the anisotropic fragmentation process. Our analysis, based on the comprehensive propagator approach, reveals significant changes in polarization at magnetic field strengths exceeding 10^18 Gauss. Notably, this effect is particularly pronounced when accounting for the anisotropic distribution of particles, which cannot be ignored in quark-gluon plasma conditions. The phenomenon may serve as a diagnostic tool to identify and analyze the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma in experimental settings, such as non-central heavy ion collisions.

Recent advances in NLP, particularly with transformer-based models, have significantly improved question-answering capabilities. Although this has led to high accuracy in various datasets, it comes at the cost of relying heavily on massive amounts of training data, which can be impractical for many real-world applications. A key issue in knowledge-based NLP tasks is handling ambiguous relationships, which often requires complex logical reasoning. In this study, we explore a novel method of integrating logical reasoning into question-answering models, and we test it on the FQABench dataset, a comprehensive collection of Facebook queries with various relationship types. Our approach involves fine-tuning a pre-trained language model on synthetic data generated by a knowledge graph reasoner, and we find that this model outperforms traditional knowledge graph embedders and achieves competitive results with large, industry-specific models.

We've developed a new method to create high-dimensional expanders using grouped structures, which enhance previously established constructions. These newly made expanders have enhanced properties and provide improved bounds in areas like the expansion of slices and codes, ultimately leading to better results with fewer variables and lower degrees.

This research examines how effectively GPT-3's prompt engineering can handle a range of tasks without prior training, categorizing them into four types: input selection, output formatting, human-like responses, and decision-making assessments. We've also developed a framework for analyzing and comparing these prompts, revealing insights into the model's decision-making accuracy and identifying areas for improvement. Our findings indicate that human-like prompts often yield superior accuracy but require more computational resources, while accuracy generally improves with an increased training dataset size.

This article builds upon prior research by O. Colmez and J. -W. Liu, exploring 
the L-invariants associated with algebraic modular forms within the framework 
of a generalised geometric motivic origin. It extends their findings to a broader 
scenario, encompassing the motives associated with Hilbert-BLuehrlet spaces.

In experiments involving quantum simulations and atom-trapping, detecting microwave signals at a distance from atoms is crucial. However, the long wavelength of these signals (centimeter to meter scale) poses a challenge for systems based on sensitive, smaller-scale electrons found in atoms. To overcome this, researchers turned to using highly charged atoms called Rydberg states, which have larger electron orbits. A new approach involves applying deep learning to analyze Rydberg states more effectively. Experiments have shown that using machine learning can identify a significant improvement - nearly 20 decibels of better sensitivity - when detecting microwaves from 52 to 77 megahertz. The research found that training on simulated data from atoms called Rubidium in an excited state gave the best results. Additionally, the research revealed an unexpected improvement in how well the atoms absorb the microwave signals, which could be due to training on artificial data rather than real-world samples.

UGC 8839 stands out as an exceptional grand-design spiral galaxy, featuring a remarkable S-shaped hyper-constant pattern in its inner regions. A detailed analysis of its properties, including radial velocity and surface brightness patterns, reveals that its inner and outer disks are not aligned. Instead, they exhibit a significant twist, with a precession angle of approximately 45 degrees. This misalignment is likely a result of a past interaction with a nearby galaxy, which may have triggered the intense star formation and starburst activity observed in UUGC 8839. This activity, in turn, may have caused the observed ionized gas flares and enhanced its magnetic fields.

This study begins with a demonstration that for almost every point in a quasicircle within C, the Hausdorff measure is non-zero when calculated over its radial limit points, utilizing an approach initially proposed by P. Shishkahev in 2009. Additionally, it's found that this result generalizes to the limits of quasiregular self-mappings defined on D, specifically DF, where D denotes the set of points in C with a finite Poisson integral. Furthermore, the houseorff measure for the limit set of an hyperbolic convex-cocyclic set is examined within C.

The occurrence of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere has been confirmed as early as 2001, and since then, multiple studies have provided compelling evidence for their presence as observed by MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN. These instruments have detected variations in atmospheric density at the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT) level, characterized by spatial scales between 50 and 500 km. This review aims to present a comprehensive summary of examined GWs at the MLT level, focusing on their detection methods via spacecraft ion and neutral mass spectrometers, and to discuss recent studies investigating the characteristics of GWs through power spectra analysis. Additionally, this review explores the impact of GWs on atmospheric density and how their propagation is influenced by diurnal variations in tides.

The LHC has demonstrated its capability to generate both photons and photons and particles with high yield in high-energy particle collisions. Research into the interaction of lead ions has yielded an enormous amount of photons-squared per ion, which has enabled scientists to create a state of ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs). These UPCs can be harnessed to investigate the properties of individual protons and lead nuclei. This paper examines UPC data collected during the 2015-2016 run at a LHC energy of 5.02 TeV, focusing on the production of J/psi particles in both lead-on-lead and proton-on-lead collisions. Our findings are in line with predictions based on quantum electrodynamics theory and the color-singlet model for gluon exchanges, with exceptions in specific scenarios. Color-singlet model calculations suggest that gluon exchanges may contribute to photon composition in heavy-ion collisions. This could be crucial for understanding the composition of photons that cause the production of J/psi particles in interactions involving saturated states known as the saturation regime.

The visual element plays a significant role in directing our attention, and sound has the potential to do the same. In this research, we propose a novel approach to automatically creating a listening experience, where users are guided to explore complex 3D environments by following audio cues. Our method builds upon and refines existing synthesis techniques, allowing us to explore the creative possibilities of sound design for multiple applications. To assist in this process, we introduce a sound system that enables us to efficiently communicate complex audio characteristics through straightforward text descriptions. Our system's flexibility is demonstrated through a series of experiments and a live sound design workshop, where participants are able to create custom audio cues for various purposes.

The application of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) has significantly impacted various domains, including computer vision, text processing and machine learning. This chapter delves into the underlying principles of RNNs, highlighting their strengths and limitations, before exploring how to effectively integrate them into computer vision tasks. It also provides a comprehensive overview of current research trends in computer vision, which leverage RNNs to address various problems.

Models comparing pandemic health costs to economic damage suggest that remote work is a suitable measure to mitigate the outbreak. Nevertheless, the correlation between an individual's virus exposure and economic value underpins this conclusion, raising the question of its universal applicability. Our research demonstrates that the optimal implementation of a uniform policy like remote work is indeed a top priority, but only under the assumption that infection risks are evenly distributed across the economy and that economic losses are directly linked to adherence to health guidelines. We also investigate under which economic and epidemiological conditions the optimal strategy shifts to a more nuanced approach, offering tailored support based on sector-specific needs.

A critical step in the process of developing a machine learning model involves fine-tuning its hyperparameters, but this can be complicated by a lack of clear guidance on which data issues might be affecting model performance. Researchers have introduced the concept of Shapley Importance for data validation, an innovative approach that utilizes Shapley value theory to assess how different data problems contribute to the model's error. By applying Shapley Value over End-to-End Machine Learning (SVOEML) models, the method can identify which issues have the greatest impact on model error without the need to create a separate meta-model for validation. We have developed an algorithm to implement SVOEML models, and through experimentation, the Shapley significance of data problems was confirmed to effectively correlate with the level of model error they introduce.
This study aims to address a specific problem: how to count solutions within a given context.

Recently, magnetic trimerization has been observed in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn, which also exhibits a weak ferromagnetism at low temperatures through spin canting. Our theoretical research finds that applying pressure can induce magnetic trimerization and enhance weak ferromagnetism in Mn$_3$Sn. Specifically, our calculations predict that applying pressure can eliminate competing helical magnetic orders and induce magnetic trimerization, alongside increasing spin canting angles due to the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. Furthermore, our theoretical model demonstrates that such pressure can amplify the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn by up to 200 times its zero-pressure counterpart, which may be attributed to the occupation of free electrons near the Fermi level.

Significant advancements in Natural Language Processing, particularly in the area of relation extraction, have been observed in recent years. This survey delves into various aspects of relation extraction, including its fundamental concepts, evaluation techniques, and applications. We also explore different approaches to enabling relations in pre-trained word embeddings and examine multiple architectures for relation extraction. By analyzing the strengths and limitations of existing methods, we discuss potential areas for further development in this field.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a specific class of nonlinear Steklov-Robin boundary value problems. Notably, we demonstrate the existence of a nontrivial solution within certain first eigenvalue intervals and prove the existence of unique positive solutions under specific Robin parameter conditions.

A hypergraph is a fundamental abstraction used to model complex systems in various fields, including natural language processing, biology, and art history. Although the theoretical applications of hypergraphs are well understood, real-world uses are hindered by the difficulty in accurately reconstructing them from fragmented data. Traditional methods fall short in building accurate hypergraphs due to the inherent noise and incompleteness of available data sources. This study presents a new approach to hypergraph reconstruction that overcomes these challenges by transforming the problem into a dual-objective optimization process. This approach ensures that the resulting hypergraph retains essential information while minimizing the impact of noise and incompleteness. To achieve this, a new, practical evaluation metric has been developed to assess reconstruction quality. This study's evaluation demonstrates the proposed method's superiority over existing reconstruction techniques.

This paper proposes an innovative approach for chest X-ray analysis by generating CT-projections from 3D CT scans, thereby enabling the creation of high-quality annotations for training and evaluation of XRAI models. These annotations include advanced features such as bounding boxes, segmentation, and point clouds, which can be extracted using cutting-edge computer vision and graphics techniques. The open-source dataset and tools we provide will facilitate the development of more accurate and interpretable XRAI models, ultimately contributing to improved medical diagnosis and treatment planning.

The Thurston norm is a concept that helps categorize surfaces within three-dimensional spaces, specifically contact manifolds. Its size, indicated by entropy, can help distinguish between different types of contact structures. We've developed an equation to calculate the Thurston norm for a particular class of contact manifolds, derived from links to positive transverse structures. This discovery allows us to use the Thurston norm and entropy together to identify and distinguish between these specific types of contact structures, particularly on certain families of manifolds like P^2 x S^1, natural connections on specific 3-torus slices and Heegaard surfaces, as well as boundary-tied structures on P^2 x S^1.

We suggest an advanced modification of a previously established entropy-based design principle for micro- and nano-photonic lasers, capable of accurately predicting directional emission in the same scenario where the thermodynamic approach fails. Experimental results from InGaAsP micro- and nanocylinder lasers, featuring an integrated grating, validate our revised methodology's effectiveness. Furthermore, our procedure can be applied to systems with complex boundaries, further outdoing the traditional thermodynamic method's limitations.

This research examines the cost fluctuations of various cryptocurrencies over time, focusing on their potential to serve as a stable means of transaction across different markets, and also investigates whether the duration of cost stability varies between currencies, as indicated by the efficient market hypothesis. Our cost stability metric is based on the distance between prices at two different times, and the currencies that exhibit cost stability at one point in time should, according to the efficient market hypothesis, show signs of arbitrage opportunities being eliminated. We found that approximately 70% of observed cost stability instances conform to the predictions of the efficient market hypothesis, and the remaining 30% can be attributed to market imperfections, such as the absence of numerous market participants, varying levels of risk, and the absence of short-selling options.

We establish that the distribution of height differences at two points, separated by distance $\ell$, follows a Gaussian pattern with a variance proportional to $\exp(-\ell/\ell_0)$ for short distances, and for long distances it is proportional to $1/\sqrt{\ell}$ with a specific decay function, where $\ell_0$ is a noise correlation length. Our findings verify that the traditional feeble noise theory holds valid in the far distance limit, and we have also determined the distribution of large height gradients. Notably, the distribution function of a height profile $h$ over a given interval, when scaled appropriately, converges as the interval size approaches infinity, and we have derived an analytical expression for its density. Our analytical results are complemented by simulation data that align with our theory, and the approach we employ can be applied to other stochastic processes as well.

Our investigation of magnetically connected solar plasma from 12:45 to 14:45 UT on April 12, 2017, revealed multiple turbulent interactions between Alfv\'en waves traveling in opposite directions. The waves' amplitudes exceeded their local mean magnetic field strength, and the resulting turbulent regions contained complex field structures with intricate field line topology. The complex interaction between the waves caused their steepening and fragmentation, leading to the development of various structures such as layers, rolls, and sheets with very sharp gradients. The observed turbulent fluctuations spanned a broad range of scales, spanning three to four orders of magnitude, and the smallest scales detected by MMS were found to share similar characteristics with the ion gyroradius, despite being a MMS potential. This suggests that the turbulent fluctuations at these smallest scales possess sufficient free energy to accelerate ions.

In certain situations, it is essential to utilize XUV and soft X-ray pulses lasting only a few hundred attoseconds or even fewer. One effective approach to achieve this involves employing electron bunches with similar temporal characteristics, which can be done by applying an altered form of the radiofrequency field using a precise resonator. This method, however, results in an uneven energy distribution among the electron bunch, necessitating an analysis of its impact on the outcome of High Energy Density Particle Sources (HEPS). Physically based estimates for the onset of flow instabilities in complex fluids have been refined and generalized. Generalized estimates of the critical Reynolds number can predict when hydrodynamic flow instabilities occur in sheared layers of any profile, for any viscosity ratio and viscosities of the mixing layers. This study confirms previous findings and discovers that the method often underestimates the critical Reynolds number, with the degree of discrepancy increasing with the critical Reynolds number itself. The approach also fails in certain conditions, such as when instability arises from a specific type of bifurcation or when two fluids with different densities are involved. However, the method can predict how the critical Reynolds number changes with the shearing flow's power law index and the viscosity ratio in cases where estimates are applicable.

Election manipulation through district boundary alteration has been a persistent issue in the US for over two centuries, with both parties accused of drawing lines in their favor. Existing methods for detecting such manipulation often rely on comparing vote distributions within districts, but this approach is limited by lack of information about alternative districting plans. Although computer algorithms can generate plausible plans, assessing their impact on vote outcomes is computationally infeasible. A new system using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method allows for the evaluation of both party bias and districting quality, taking into account historical voting patterns. This method identifies severe cases of manipulation in real US election data and also detects the effects of the 2000 Bush-Gore election manipulation in Florida.

The assessment of patterned textile quality is a complex task, as many flaws are camouflaged by patterns. Researchers have proposed using GHOG, a method that can effectively identify such concealed defects. However, this approach often yields a noisy detection map, primarily due to the significant difference in feature descriptors between different flaw types and the intricate designs. This research presents an enhanced method that combines the advantages of GHOG with the benefits of a matrix decomposition technique, thereby streamlining and accelerating the defect detection process. By reducing the variation in feature descriptor space, the method refines the detection map, and further improves it through a post-processing step that leverages a low-rank matrix and sparse matrix combination to distinguish defects from the background.

In recent years, deep reinforcement learning has become the leading approach for fully autonomous navigation systems. Nevertheless, these systems often struggle to generalize well across various environments, especially those with limited or no prior knowledge, and their performance tends to degrade significantly when trained from scratch. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel architecture that integrates information theory to guide the learning process. By using this structure, we enable the agent to adapt its behavior to different geometric configurations, regardless of the specific training scenario. Furthermore, we introduce a new training method based on intrinsic motivation to further enhance generalization capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving improved generalization, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques in numerous public navigation datasets.

This study establishes a specific restriction, known as Bondi mass-reduction limit, which sets the minimum rate at which asymptotically flat spacetimes can lose mass to gravitational waves. The theory's mathematical foundation is built upon initial data that adheres to the Einstein equations, and the findings confirm the existence of an irreversible process in gravitational wave phenomena. As a result, certain initial conditions preclude the complete cessation of gravitational wave emission. The research also provides a formula for calculating the upper bound of energy output from binary black hole mergers, which was found to be approximately 0.12 percent of the total system mass, and existing numerical simulations are in close agreement with this theoretical prediction.

The initial population of stars, formed shortly after the Big Bang, in early galaxies likely produced numerous black holes. These black holes may now reside within the dense central regions of some galaxies, known as Nuclear Star Clusters. By creating a detailed numerical model, we've found that early galaxies with populations of the initial black holes would result in detectable gravitational waves. These waves would be detectable by LIGO, but more certainly by future space-based detectors like LISA. This research provides a map to pinpoint the sources of these gravitational waves, allowing us to track their direction and distance. This information can be used to study the properties of the first stars and their galaxies, providing a link between the study of gravitational waves and the study of the early universe.

This paper introduces a data-driven method to detect and localize incidents in power distribution networks by utilizing SCADA measurements and assuming a single incident at a time. The approach can handle both radial and reconfigured radial topologies, as well as various measurement setups, including meter placement and phasor data from phasor measurement units. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of the 123-bus test system.

The decay of the $X(3872)$ into $J/\psi \pi \gamma$ is investigated using both electromagnetic and strong interactions, with a calculated electromagnetic contribution that aligns with experimental observations. This result supports the interpretation of $X(3872)$ as a $D^0 D^{*0}$ molecule, with its dominant decay into $\bar{D}_0 D^{*0}$ linked to a charge-conjugation eigenvalue of $+1$. Additionally, a process where $X(3872)$ decays into $J/\psi$ and two soft pions or kaons is investigated, with calculated rates that align with experimental findings and further support its understanding as a $D^0 D^{*0}$ state.

We establish a definition for a specific type of embedded variety, called $\mathcal{Q}$, characterized by a collection of axioms. It's demonstrated that any isotropic subspace of a non-degenerate quadratic space meets these characterization criteria. Furthermore, in the context of a field with a characteristic other than 2, all varieties embedded quads are shown to be equivalent to the isotropic subgrassmannian through an isomorphism. The proof leverages the properties of symplectic group action and subsequent induction, along with a derived formula for $\mathcal{Q}$ utilizing linear sections. Lastly, the concept of a quadric being dominated by another is defined, which ultimately leads to the statement that any quadric can be represented as a projection of a hyperbolic quadric.

Text-based games provide a reliable platform to assess advanced NLP models by comparing them to classic control agents.
One key challenge in mastering text-based games is the significant sample inefficiency, which often requires millions of training examples.
A recent breakthrough enables high-speed simulation training at a rate of one million steps per second, facilitating rapid imitation learning for complex games.
A new game platform, TextWorldExpress, is introduced to streamline the development of text-based games and provide a standard interface for testing the effectiveness of modern learning algorithms.
The platform's capabilities are demonstrated by achieving state-of-the-art results in both simulated and imitated settings, including complex tasks like cooking and chess that previous methods struggled to solve.

Insulating behaviors in Topological Insulators can be characterized by distinct properties. 
These properties can be distinctly identified using spatially dependent or independent methods. 
However, utilizing spatially dependent phase functions poses a challenge due to ambiguities that arise at samples with non-trivial features. 
These ambiguities can be resolved by partitioning the sample into various sections, but this partitioning process may introduce unnecessary complications. 
A novel, more straightforward approach is presented here to describe and classify Topological Insulators without spatial considerations. 
This approach is particularly suitable for samples exhibiting non-trivial features.

The paper focuses on investigating non-linear eigenvalue problems involving the $p$-Laplace problem in sectors with various angles within the plane, particularly examining how the behavior of these problems changes when the sector angle is small and $p$ is close to one. To achieve this investigation, we establish a new approach for analyzing eigenfunctions of the $p$-Laplace problem in sectors, which involves the concept of sector viscosity eigenfunctions. Using this approach, we derive several precise estimates for eigenfunctions and their associated eigenvalue bounds in sectors, which hold under certain conditions related to the sector angle and the value of $p$. These estimates enable us to understand how the eigenfunctions behave when approaching the boundary of the sector and how their growth is limited by specific power functions. Ultimately, our findings provide a detailed analysis of how the behavior of $p$-harmonic functions in sectors is influenced by both the value of $p$ and the geometry of the sector, which has implications for understanding related problems in mathematical physics and partial differential equations.

This research introduces a novel spatial extreme value model capable of describing the peak occurrences of sea levels within various ocean regions simultaneously. The implementation of Copulas enables flexibility in modeling peak events. The analysis involves parameter estimation through simulation-based methods and assessing model fit using statistical tests. Additionally, this study forecasts the most intense future sea level extremes in different ocean areas. A case study utilizing Sea Level Exceedances across six New Zealand locations illustrates the application and effectiveness of the proposed model.

Let $k$ be a non-algebraically closed field and $X$ an irreducible, complete variety defined over $k$. It's known that if we consider the set of $k$-rational points on $X$, this set is finite and consists of only constant functions. However, if $X$ is a non-constant morphism from $ \mathbb{P}^1_k$ to $\mathbb{P}^n_k$, there exists an infinite set of $k$-rational points on $X$.

In collaborative tasks between humans and robots, the robot must be able to interpret and respond to human movements within its own understanding of the task environment. For this to happen, the robot needs to align its task model with the human's intended actions. When a human guides a robot using a tether, the forces they exert on it can be used to identify their relative movements through model-based identification. However, simply averaging human and robot movements can result in distorted movements that don't reflect the human's intended actions. To resolve this issue, this study proposes a method to transfer skills from humans to robots by using a closed-loop icp algorithm that takes into account the specific constraints of the task while optimizing a cost function that minimizes the difference between human and robot movements in a space that's more relevant to the task. The proposed method was tested on a mobile manipulator in a series of experiments involving object placement and manipulation, and the results show that it successfully transfers human skills to robots in a way that preserves the specific patterns of movement.

This research employs the matrix element technique in conjunction with parton shower to examine the Higgs boson pair production process, specifically the $\textrm{b}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ decay channel, using the F*{o}rtran On-shell Matrix Element event generator, and compares it to the result from the Next-to-Leading Log approximation, and discusses the implications for detector-level comparisons.

Our approach employs self-supervision to train robots to grasp rotating objects. A novel feature extraction method allows the robot to identify and predict the position of a target feature on an object in 3D space. By accurately segmenting objects and distinguishing their properties, our system also improves error detection when objects are grasped. When combined with a novel reward mechanism that penalizes the rotation of the grabbed object, our robot successfully operates and human motion data further accelerates task learning via pre-training.

The rapid dissemination of false information on social media has a significant impact, particularly when it comes to public health initiatives such as COVID-19 vaccination campaigns. Research indicates that misinformation can hinder vaccine acceptance and foster conspiracy theories. A key factor in understanding this phenomenon is analyzing how individual tweets in a conversation are evaluated. Our study introduces a novel task that examines how people respond to COVID-19 vaccination-related misinformation within the context of Twitter conversations. This study draws inspiration from research on misinformation and Twitter discussions, aiming to identify how tweets in a conversation are ultimately accepted, rejected, or remain neutral in sentiment. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of this new task and showcases the effectiveness of various text-based and multimodal models in performing this task.

A key goal in attosecond science is producing isolated attosecond pulse trains (APTNTs) via high harmonic generation (HHG) driven by a few-cycle infrared field. However, the emission spectrum from an experimental setup is affected by the central carrier-envelope phase (CEP) of the driving laser, a parameter that is prone to instability. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel approach to manipulate attosecond pulses on an attosecond scale using a complex infrared field, achieved through the use of a plasma mirror. By leveraging a numerical model, we have demonstrated the feasibility of our method, showing that it enables precise control over the emission time, independent of the laser's central CEP.

We've conducted a comprehensive study of companion candidates in binary systems
associated with Nova Aquillae 1968. Our analysis involved obtaining high-resolution
spectra of the Al8 giant of Nova Aquillae 1968 using the VLT/USSP and the VLT/UVES
instrument, and we observed that its profile matches the characteristics of a typical
post-outburst system. This is in contrast to previous findings that suggested the presence
of a companion. By examining the VLT/USSP and VLT/UVES data, we failed to detect any
companion signals, and we propose possible explanations for this outcome. Additionally,
we explored the possibility of a companion with an unusual spectral type or very low
mass. Our study also involved a search for companion candidates in other post-outburst systems
of similar mass, such as Nova Delphini 2011 and Nova Aquillae 2018.

We are considering a time-dependent, complex-valued function $u(t,x)$ defined for $t\geq 0$ and $x\in\Omega$, a given bounded and convex region in the $d$-dimensional space with a smooth boundary. This function is intended to solve the given initial-value problem involving the Schrödinger equation with a power nonlinear term of $1+(2\delta/d)$-order, subject to the Dirichlet boundary condition and an initial value $\phi$ within the $H^1_0(\Omega)$ function space. Our analysis focuses on the conditions under which the solution becomes unbounded in a specific norm as time progresses. By assuming the initial value $\phi$ has sufficient high frequency content, we have demonstrated the existence of such explosive solutions for $\delta$ values within the range of $[1,\infty)$ when the dimension $d$ is at least five, and $\delta$ equals one when the dimension is four.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional numerical methods by integrating physical laws into a neural network that uses automatic differentiation to solve partial differential equations. However, there are concerns regarding the accuracy and efficiency of PINNs in certain problem types, such as forward problems with low to moderate conditioning. Recent research introduced a Residual-based Adaptive Grid generation method for Neural Networks (RAG) to dynamically adjust the solution domain, but it has limitations in handling complex problems in higher dimensions. We developed an improved method, Residual-based ANG (RANG), which considers not only domain residuals but also solution gradients and problem characteristics. By applying RANG to benchmark problems, we observed significant improvements in the location and distribution of solution points, leading to enhanced accuracy and reduced training time, while also addressing issues of neural network over-parameterization.

This study introduces a comprehensive simulation framework for subthreshold conduction in multi-domain FeFETs, incorporating the concept of adverse capacitance arising from domain walls. By dividing the channel into triangular prism segments, we apply the finite element method to solve for scalar magnetic potentials and vectorial electric fields. Our analysis reveals that adverse capacitance arises from electric field distortions near domain walls, which significantly impact the fe-field product within the channel. Moreover, we break down adverse capacitance into horizontal and vertical components, discovering that vertical adverse capacitance dominates the channel's electric field. This research also addresses the adverse Coulomb potential and explores how adverse electrical work influences the FeFET's subthreshold behavior.

A dynamic freight ecosystem is comprised of interconnected entities, with each entity characterized by unique attributes, contributing to its distinctiveness. To provide innovative solutions for optimizing the freight ecosystem, there is a pressing need to gain a deeper understanding of its structure and function. To achieve this, we suggest developing a specialized knowledge graph that maps the relationships between key freight ecosystem components. Our proposed framework involves a two-stage process. Firstly, we outline a systematic approach to constructing the freight ecosystem knowledge graph. Secondly, we utilize this generated graph to analyze weakness propagation. Our study's initial phase involved defining entity types, relationship categories, and attribute data. Our initial findings demonstrate the utility of this knowledge graph in identifying and tracking entity weaknesses. Our analysis reveals that weaknesses in freight ecosystem entities can have a significant impact on overall system performance.

The paper's main goal is to examine the irreducibility of a certain class of stochastic partial differential equations, specifically the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subject to pure jump noise. It is assumed that these equations occur on a 2D or higher 空间 bounded domain. To achieve this, we first establish a relevant ergodic property. This is accomplished through an analysis of the corresponding deterministic equations, for which we establish a key surjectivity result. This result enables us to identify a specific type of control, allowing for arbitrary trajectories. This control theory approach, combined with the use of Itō calculus techniques, forms the foundation of our argument.

Given a group G, its associated power graph $\Gamma_{\sim}(G)$ can be constructed using elements $x$ and $y$ where $x$ is a positive power of $x$. The minimum chromosome length of G, denoted $\ell(G)$, is the maximum length of the shortest paths that generate G. In this context, we investigate power graphs of non-trivial nilpotent groups to determine a condition related to a specific type of subgroups, and calculate a maximum value for $\ell(G)$ in terms of a specific type of subgroups. Furthermore, we establish a theorem that provides a maximum value for $\ell(G)$ in terms of a specific type of subgroups, and identify cases in which this maximum value is achieved.

A proposal to upgrade the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is presented, focusing on significantly enhancing its capabilities to study the properties of the strong interaction in the non-perturbative region and investigating cosmic radiation physics. This proposal outlines a potential LHC attachment that could dramatically expand the data collection capacity, thereby enabling a vast array of research opportunities within the LHC's and non-terrestrial energy ranges.

A general framework, orientation convolutional networks (O-CN), is developed to create convolutional neural networks that respect rotational and reflectional symmetry in their inputs. This is achieved by assigning consistent weights to an operation based on its geometric effect, which can be applied to various baseline architectures. As a result, G-O-CN produces a compact, feature-rich tensor with reduced redundancy. This approach is particularly effective in medical imaging applications, where it achieves high performance with fewer parameters. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that G-O-CN has a substantial ability to generalize from training data to unseen, input transformations.

Recent advancements in learning-based methods, particularly graph convolutional networks (GCNs), have led to notable success in point cloud processing. However, the inherent irregularities of raw point cloud data pose significant challenges for GCNs in learning effective patterns. To address these issues, we have developed a new approach that enhances GCUs through two key strategies. Firstly, we employ advanced normalization and activation techniques to improve the stability of GCUs and enable more robust learning. Secondly, we introduce a novel architecture that adapts the depth of GCUs based on the geometric characteristics of the point cloud, thereby optimizing performance. Our method demonstrates superior results over existing techniques and provides a framework for further exploration in point cloud processing.

One effective method to detect traditional code change assaults is through static or dynamic comparison of binaries, but this method fails to uncover hostless trojans that are hidden within the binary code and expressed through high-level programming languages. To address this gap, a new detection strategy is proposed that involves analyzing the semantic meaning of the code using a neural network-based model, which compares the legitimate and malicious versions of the software to identify any discrepancies in their operational functions. The code is first transformed into a series of meaningful phrases, which are then mapped to a network of interconnected nodes, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the software's underlying logic and syntax. The semantic changes are calculated using a measure of dissimilarity between the corresponding nodes in the code's neural network representation. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a series of experiments that successfully identify hostless trojans by matching the code's semantic structure with its corresponding functionality.

We present an update on the installation progress of the four-imager integral field unit, ROSIE, on the Magellan IMACS imager at the Magellan Telescopes. Initially designed and constructed at the University of Washington, this integral field spectrometer has undergone initial testing on the vector-magellan telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory in Chile during 2022. Due to a manufacturing issue discovered during commissioning, development of the instrument was paused until the problem was resolved. As a result of acquiring a replacement grating, the instrument's installation on the remaining three imagers has been delayed. We now discuss the current status of the project, the obtained optical and spectrographic performance results, and its anticipated completion timeline.

Our research has re-evaluated the fusion of carbon-12 with carbon-12 at deep subbarrier energies, and we found that it aligns with predictions from the tunneling model, particularly considering the formation of compound nuclei. Notably, at lower collision energies, the impact of di-nucleon transfer processes overrides the influence of tunneling effects. Additionally, the analysis revealed that at very low collision energies, Condon-Moses systemation effectively describes the fusion process. Furthermore, this study offers an improved method for tunneling effects in Trojan horse factor calculations, crucial for nuclear reaction studies at low collision energies.

Identifying and characterizing exoplanets is a major goal in astronomy, with a key focus on Earth-like planets. Their masses and sizes can be measured, but their internal compositions and structures are still unclear. The interior of a rocky planet is influenced by its mass, radius, and the chemical makeup of its building blocks. To gain insight into these factors, a study was conducted on the internal dynamics of three rocky planets, using the observed mass and radius data along with the chemical composition of their host stars from the CARMENES Legacy Program. The chemical analysis of the host stars, combined with the known mass and radius of the planets, allowed the researchers to determine the internal compositions and structures of the planets. The study found that the mass-radius relationship is not straightforward and depends on the planet's mass and composition. The research also highlighted the importance of the planet's mass and composition in determining its internal structure.

Developing accurate indoor localization systems via wireless signals is complicated due to the multi-path effect, which causes significant distortions and variations in channel access. However, attention to details in capturing attentional features can mitigate these challenges and enhance performance. Consequently, we propose an attention-based model, specifically the Attentional Channel Attentional Module (ACAM), designed to extract key information from raw Channel State Information (CSI) data. By doing so, we can identify and focus on the most relevant features for improved indoor localization. By training ACAM on a dataset, we can fine-tune it for two primary tasks: (1) identifying and filtering attentional features from raw CSI, and (2) utilizing these features for indoor localization. By applying ACAM to two widely used protocols, iperf and http, we demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving superior performance compared to existing methods.

This work proposes a comprehensive framework for reasoning modally by linking various topological structures to their corresponding modal logics through the Harrop principle. The principle characterizes formulas with restricted quantifier usage, which we interpret within sheaf toposes as having fixed support. The upper and lower power sheaf toposes are used to define and unify the modal logics derived from general topological spaces and preordered spaces. The resulting comodalities allow for the relationships between these systems to be better understood.

A graph's edges can be modified by changing their colors to produce a color-altered graph. We are interested in a type of edge modification where the resulting graph has only one unusual vertex with odd-degree edges. Not all graphs can be changed in this way, but all bipartite graphs with at least one vertex can, if they have at least one edge. The specific case of changing a graph with only one column of edges in a grid-like structure has been an open question, until recently when a counter-example was found that answers 'no'.

On a group G of size n, let f be a function taking values in the range [-1, 1]. We define the function f to have a restricted Fourier spectrum if its Fourier coefficients at indices above 1 are bounded by 1. Under this condition, we prove that the minimum possible sum of adjacent pairs of f is equal to -sqrt(1). This proof also confirms a conjecture proposed by Kozen and Snir in 1985.

COPASI, a widely-used software tool for computational modeling in biology, has demonstrated its effectiveness across various domains, including qualitative investigation and quantitative simulation. However, accessing COPASI's full potential requires users to have extensive knowledge of its API and development experience with Java. To make investigating biological systems via COPASI more accessible, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based application that provides an intuitive interface for utilizing COPASI's features. By combining ease of use with powerful functionality, ShinyCOPASI enables users to quickly set up simulations, analyze results, and share them with others, all while maintaining the depth of COPASI's capabilities.

One of the core principles of science is that findings should be replicable. This value has significant implications for artificial intelligence as well. Deep learning models, however, are frequently evaluated based on efficiency and performance, often overlooking concerns related to accuracy and reliability. As a result, overfitting can lead to unreliable predictions. Ambiguity measures are tools that assess the uncertainty of machine learning models, similar to scientific practices. They are crucial for verifying the accuracy of models, detecting data overfitting, and building more trustworthy systems. This study introduces ambiguity measurement in the context of machine learning, explores various methods, and provides a comprehensive comparison of these techniques using comprehensive datasets.
We establish the type of the von Neumann algebra generated by unitary type functions within a non-commutative group.

The combination of the iterative relaxation strategy iteration and the generalized minimal residual method has been shown effective in solving large-scale Markov decision processes, yet it still suffers from a slow convergence rate when dealing with numerous states. We propose a novel modification to this approach by introducing an imprecise GMRES method, which accelerates its rate of convergence. By imposing fewer constraints on residual vectors, the imprecise GMRES method generates a smaller residual subspace, allowing for the selection of a more optimal solution correction and thus improving solution accuracy. Our analysis demonstrates that the solution found using the imprecise GMRES method falls within an $\epsilon$-radius of the optimal solution, and based on this theory, we implement the strategy and develop the I-ISMGMRES algorithm. Our numerical results using random and traffic light MDP models confirm that the proposed strategy yields better results than the standard GMRES and dense iterative relaxation Strategy Iteration methods, particularly in terms of finding a viable solution when others fail to converge within a set maximum iteration limit.

Consider a directed weighted graph G, defined by vertices arranged in a row and columns, where each edge connects adjacent elements. We demonstrate that the g-th symbolic power of the associated ideal I_G is equal to the normal power (I_G)^{g+1}. This finding generalizes the previously established result for G being a simple directed path. Moreover, we examine a scenario in which G deviates minimally from a line graph, and prove that I_G's symbolic and symbolic square powers coincide only under specific conditions.

Computer simulations, particularly those involving complex systems like climate change, offer a valuable way to understand the underlying mechanisms of these systems. For example, adjusting variables in an atmospheric model can reveal how different factors contribute to global warming. However, it's often difficult to reverse-engineer these contributions from the model outputs due to their interconnected nature. Researchers have developed methods to analyze realistic model data, but these approaches are computationally expensive and ineffective for noisy or imperfect data. In this paper, we introduce a new, more efficient method for reversing this process by analyzing time series data, leveraging mathematical equations to identify a multivariate relationship between the model outputs and the unknown variables' contributions. This involves estimating multiple two-dimensional surfaces and can be easily applied using standard techniques. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not require direct access to the system being modeled and provides a more accurate representation of the model's data by accounting for its inherent noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through examples, including analyzing a well-known climate model and the output of a random process.

Achieving robust generalization in complex tasks is a significant challenge in artificial intelligence. One effective strategy to address this is dividing the learning process into regional groups, where each group learns characteristic skills for tasks within its region. However, it's not clear under what conditions this approach works best. We investigate this by establishing theoretical conditions for it to be beneficial and experimentally verifying these conditions. Our study demonstrates that it's not simply having multiple environments that makes regional learning beneficial; rather, it's the variation in required skills within those environments. Additionally, we found that grouping similar environments together can hinder learning, and we observe this effect across different modeling methods.

The Connaissance experiment at the LHC has analyzed jets formed in conjunction with isolated photons in 2015 data, measuring how jet transverse momentum and asymmetry are altered in center-of-mass collisions with a 5.02 TeV energy. Comparing jets from proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, we found that as lead-lead centrality increases, the number of high-momentum jets decreases and their average transverse momentum drops below that of proton-proton collisions. Notably, these effects are more pronounced for jets at lower transverse momentum thresholds. Furthermore, average jet asymmetry values show no significant difference from proton-proton collisions up to a transverse momentum of 450 GeV, with a slight increase observed at lower centrality and larger values at lower momentum.

This paper provides direct proof that certain non-alterning multiple zeta values can be expressed as a combination of colored zeta values, and also establishes a new identity resembling Ap\'{e}ry's famous theorem.

A thorough study of an unusual brown dwarf, known as WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, has been conducted, revealing key details about its nature. Comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic observations, combined with accurate radial velocity measurements, have allowed for accurate estimates of the object's temperature, temperature range, and effective temperature. Its low surface gravity has also been determined, and its mass has been estimated. Notably, the brown dwarf's unusually cool temperature, combined with its high metal content, has resulted in a significant excess of molecular bands in its spectrum. Additionally, the presence of a close companion star, which was not taken into account in earlier studies, has significantly altered our understanding of the brown dwarf's nature.

Our findings from the rapidity range of $|y| < 0.5$ for midrapidity production in a 5.44 TeV Xe-Xe collision are presented in this document. Key measurements include the overall production rates, both inclusive and differential transverse momentum distributions, and two-particle correlations with varying p_T and rapidity cut-offs.

We propose an approach to interpolate and extrapolate universal parton distribution functions utilizing their effective low-x behavior, effective high-x behavior, and known experimental data points. The method leverages the PDFs' distinct characteristics at low and high values of x to improve interpolation accuracy. Our findings also reveal that a specific set of model-based parameters can accurately predict the PDFs across a broad range of scales without needing to retrain the model.

Space exploration missions face significant obstacles in constructing habitats and deploying surface vehicles due to the limited understanding of utilizing local regolith for construction purposes. Research has shown that sintering can effectively utilize the natural glass-forming properties within planetary soils to create in-situ built structures using heat sources from solar radiation or nuclear power. This study investigates the effect of different sintering temperatures on the microstructure and mechanical properties of Martian and Lunar moldes samples. By subjecting the samples to heat sources of 800°C and 1200°C for one hour, the results indicate that the optimal compression strength for both the lunar and martian samples was achieved at 800°C. Furthermore, the samples created using the lunar mission showed superior mechanical properties in comparison to the samples created using the martian mission.

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability is analyzed in a liquid layer that forms on a fiber with a specific geometry, where the contact point is prevented from moving along the fiber due to a barrier. A theoretical model, based on a combination of lubrication theory and capillary theory, is used to understand the instability. This analysis reveals that when the barrier is very close to the equator of the fiber, the critical wavelength becomes significantly longer, and the onset time is much slower. A second approach, which considers slow viscous flow, yields the same results, and is found to be more accurate.
